title: Never learned to cook? Where to start as an adult (and why recipes go wrong)
description: A simple order to learn the basics in, the kit you actually need, and the most common reasons a recipe fails for beginners.
intro: Plenty of adults never learned to cook at home. You don't need talent, just a sensible order and a few repeat dinners.

list: A large frying pan, a saucepan with a lid, a baking tray, a sharp knife, a chopping board, a wooden spoon and a timer. That's enough for months.
Eggs (boiled, scrambled, fried), then rice and pasta, so you learn heat and timing.
Roasting vegetables on a tray, then a simple pasta sauce.
A stir fry, then a one-pot stew or chilli, then a roast chicken.
The pan is too hot or not hot enough: medium heat suits most beginner cooking.
Everything is crowded into one pan, so food steams instead of browning.
Ingredients aren't prepared before you start; chop and measure first.
Seasoning only at the end: add a little salt as you go and taste.
Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food, and wash hands and boards after handling it.
Cook chicken until it's steaming hot all the way through, with no pink meat and clear juices.
Cool leftover rice quickly, keep it in the fridge, and reheat it only once.

p: Cook each dish two or three times before trying the next. After each attempt, note one thing that went wrong and one thing to change.

title: Your renewal price went up? How to get it down (UK insurance, broadband and mobile)
description: What to check, what to say on the call, and when to switch instead, plus the UK rules on renewal pricing and end-of-contract notices.
intro: Renewal quotes often arrive higher than last year's. A few minutes of checking before the date usually pays off. This is general information, not financial advice.

list: Find the renewal date and last year's price, and note what's changed in the cover or excess.
Get a like-for-like quote from a comparison site and, for insurance, a new-customer quote from your own insurer for the same cover and excess.
Since January 2022, UK home and motor insurers can't charge a renewing customer more than they'd charge an equivalent new customer through the same channel (online, phone and so on).
Broadband, mobile and pay-TV providers must tell you 10 to 40 days before your contract ends what you pay now, what you'll pay after, and their best deals.
"My renewal is £X, up from £Y last year. I've been quoted £Z for the same cover elsewhere. Can you match it, or I'll switch?"
Be polite, have the quote reference ready, and ask whether the price includes any add-ons you don't need.

p: If they won't match, switching is often simpler than haggling. Check cover, excess and any cancellation fees first, and set the new policy to start the day the old one ends.
Keep one list of every renewal date and set a reminder about four weeks before each one, so you're never rushed into auto-renewing.

title: How to write your life story for your grandchildren (and actually finish it)
description: Small weekly prompts, a simple chapter plan and a few tricks to get unstuck, so your memories become a book the family can keep.
intro: Many people start a memoir for the family and stall after a few pages. Small, regular pieces get further than waiting for a free week.

list: Answer one question a week in a few paragraphs, such as your first school, your first job, or the house you grew up in.
Write as you'd talk to a grandchild. Plain words are best; you can tidy up later.
Early childhood and family.
School days and friends.
Work, moving away and early adulthood.
Love, family and the places you've lived.
Things you'd like them to know.

p: Keep one notebook or phone note for memories as they pop up, and file them into a chapter once a week so the pile never becomes a jumble.
A photo next to a story brings it to life. Name the people and places, and give a rough year.
Set a finish date, such as a birthday. When each chapter has a few stories, put it together as a simple book or PDF. A finished short book is worth more than a perfect one that never gets done.

title: Boxes of old family photos? A simple plan to sort and digitise them
description: Tackle one envelope at a time, scan prints with your phone or a service, label faces while someone still knows them, and share the results.
intro: Old prints feel overwhelming because there are so many. Breaking them into small batches, and labelling as you go, is what gets the job finished.

list: Work one box or envelope at a time, at a table you can leave set up.
Make three piles: keep and scan, keep but don't scan, and give to a relative. Skip blurry shots and scenery nobody can place.
Phone scanning apps work well for prints: use soft, even light and avoid glare.
A flatbed scanner gives better results for precious photos; 600 dpi is a common choice for small prints.
Slides and negatives need a film scanner or a scanning service. Services charge per photo, so sort first to keep the cost down.

p: Add who, where and roughly when to each photo. Send a 'who is this?' list to older relatives now; that knowledge is the hardest thing to replace.

list: Keep at least two copies of the scans in different places, such as a cloud service and an external drive.
Share a family album so everyone can see the results and add names.

p: Fifteen minutes a few times a week adds up. Track how many boxes are done, so you can see the end.

title: How to find a pension from an old job (even if the company has closed)
description: Rebuild your job list, use the free government Pension Tracing Service, write to providers, and keep every pot on one page. UK guide.
intro: Many people have several workplace pensions from old jobs and have lost track of some. Finding them is free; it mostly takes a list and a few letters. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.h: Make a list of every job
list: Write down each employer, roughly when you worked there, and the town. Old payslips, P60s, CVs and emails help.
Note any pension paperwork or provider names you remember.
The government's Pension Tracing Service (on GOV.UK) gives you contact details for a workplace or personal pension scheme, even if the employer has closed or changed its name.
It doesn't tell you whether you have a pension or how much it's worth. You then contact the scheme.
Give your full name, any previous names and addresses, your National Insurance number, date of birth and dates of employment.
Ask whether you have benefits, their current value, and to update your address.

p: Record each pot's provider, reference number, latest value and the address they hold for you. Update it whenever you move house.

sections.h: Before you move or combine pensions
p: Check for exit fees, guarantees and valuable benefits you could lose. If a defined benefit (final salary) pension is worth more than £30,000, you must take regulated financial advice before transferring it. MoneyHelper offers free, impartial guidance.

title: How much spending money should you take on holiday? A simple way to work it out
description: Estimate a daily amount from meals, drinks, trips and treats, add a buffer, and keep track as you go so the money lasts the whole trip.
intro: There's no single right figure, because it depends on where you go and how you like to holiday. A simple daily estimate gets you close, and tracking it as you go stops nasty surprises at home.

list: Meals: how many you'll eat out each day, times a typical local price for each person.
Drinks, snacks and coffee.
Local transport, such as taxis, buses and car parking.
Extras: souvenirs, tips and the odd treat.
Price any excursions or attractions separately, and pre-book them if that's cheaper.
Add 10-20% on top for things you didn't plan for.

p: Check what your card charges abroad. Many people use a fee-free travel card and carry a small amount of local cash for places that don't take cards. Always pay in the local currency when a card machine asks.
Divide what's left by the days remaining each evening. If you overspend one day, you'll see it early and can have a cheaper day tomorrow, rather than running short at the end.
Note what you actually spent and on what. Next year's estimate will be much more accurate.

title: How to avoid being charged for hire-car damage you didn't cause
description: What to photograph at pick-up and drop-off, what to ask for at the desk, and what to do if a damage bill arrives weeks later.
intro: Disputes over hire-car damage usually come down to evidence. A few minutes with your phone at both ends of the hire makes a big difference. This is general information, not legal advice.

list: Walk round the car before you drive off and photograph every panel, the wheels and tyres, the windscreen, the roof and the interior.
Take a slow video too, and capture the fuel gauge and mileage.
Make sure every existing mark is on the damage sheet, and ask staff to sign it if anything is missing.

p: Dark car parks and rain hide scratches. If you can't see properly, ask to move the car into better light, and note the conditions.

list: Take the same photos and video in the same order, in daylight if you can.
Ask for the car to be checked with you and for a signed return report. If nobody is there, photograph the car where you left it and the key drop.
Ask the hire firm for its photos, the repair invoice and the check-out and return reports.
Reply in writing with your dated photos and video.
If you paid by credit or debit card and the charge isn't justified, ask your card provider about a chargeback, and check whether your excess insurance covers it.

p: Keep your booking, damage sheet, photos and any messages in one place for a few months after each hire, since some charges arrive weeks later.

title: Saddle stitching uneven or slanted only on one side? Common causes and fixes
description: Why hand-stitched leather looks crooked or different front to back, and simple habits that make every stitch match.
intro: Uneven saddle stitching usually comes from small inconsistencies repeated hundreds of times. Fix one habit at a time on scrap leather and compare both sides.

p: Decide which needle goes through each hole first (for example, always the back needle) and keep it the same for the whole seam. Switching changes the slant.

sections.h: Cast the same way each time
p: Before pulling the second needle through, loop (cast) the thread the same way around the first needle on every stitch. Inconsistent casting makes some stitches lie flat and others slant.

sections.h: Keep your irons and holes straight
list: Mark a stitch line with a groover or wing divider, and keep the irons upright and in line with it.
If you widen holes with an awl, hold it at the same angle every time.

p: Pull both threads with the same force after every stitch, and set each stitch the same way. Too tight on one side pulls the line crooked.

sections.h: Check both sides as you go
p: Look at the back every few stitches. Photographing both sides of a practice seam makes patterns easy to spot.

title: Filling in the PIP form: how to describe what you struggle with
description: Plain tips for the PIP 'How your disability affects you' form: honest examples, the reliability questions, evidence, deadlines and free help.
intro: The PIP form asks how your condition affects everyday activities. Clear, honest examples from real life help the assessor understand. This is general information, not advice; free help is available from Citizens Advice and local welfare rights services.

sections.h: Think about most days, not just your best
p: Describe how you manage most of the time, including bad days and how often they happen. Don't describe only your best day.

list: For each activity, ask yourself whether you can do it safely, to an acceptable standard, as often as you need to, and in a reasonable time.
If you need help, an aid, prompting or much longer than most people, say so, and say what happens if you try anyway (pain, tiredness, falls, anxiety).
Write what happened, when, how long it took, and who helped or saw it.
Keeping a short diary for a week or two before you fill in the form makes this much easier.
Send copies of letters, reports, prescription lists and anything from people who support you. Keep copies of everything.
The form has a return deadline. If you need more time, contact the DWP before it passes.

p: Citizens Advice, local welfare rights services and disability charities can help you fill in the form for free. In Scotland, new claims are for Adult Disability Payment instead of PIP.

title: Sweating through your shirts? What helps day to day, and when to see a GP
description: Practical everyday steps for heavy sweating: antiperspirant timing, fabrics and colours, a spare-top kit, tracking triggers, and when to get it checked.
intro: Heavy sweating is common and can be embarrassing, but there's a lot you can do day to day. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: You've sweated more than usual for a long time, or it's affecting your daily life or confidence.
It started suddenly, happens at night, or comes with other symptoms such as weight loss or a high temperature.
A pharmacist can also advise on stronger antiperspirants before you see a doctor.
Antiperspirant (not just deodorant) reduces sweat; deodorant only masks smell.
Many people find it works better applied to dry skin at night, so it has time to work before the next day. Follow the product's instructions.
Loose fits and breathable fabrics such as cotton, linen or moisture-wicking sportswear.
Dark colours, white, and patterns show sweat less than light grey or pale blue.
A thin undershirt can protect outer shirts.

p: Keep a small kit with a spare top, wipes and antiperspirant for interviews, presentations and events, so you're not worrying all day.
For two weeks, note when and where you sweat and what was happening: heat, stress, spicy food, caffeine, alcohol, exercise. Patterns help you plan, and the notes are useful if you see a GP.

title: How to stop junk mail and post for previous occupants (UK)
description: The free opt-outs for addressed junk mail, leaflets and charity mail, plus what to do with post for people who no longer live at your address.
intro: You can cut most junk mail with a few free opt-outs, though some takes a few months to stop. This guide covers the UK; other countries have similar registers.

list: Register with the Mailing Preference Service (MPS). It's free and reduces addressed advertising mail from companies that use it. It can take up to four months to take full effect.
Contact companies directly and ask them to remove you from their mailing list.
Royal Mail delivers some unaddressed leaflets ('door to door'). You can opt out by contacting Royal Mail; the opt-out lasts two years.
A polite 'no junk mail or leaflets' sign on your door helps with other distributors, though not everyone follows it.

p: The Fundraising Preference Service lets you stop contact from specific charities.

list: Write 'Not known at this address' or 'Return to sender' on the envelope, without opening it, and put it back in a post box.
For repeat senders, contact them directly and ask them to update their records. Don't open someone else's post.

p: Note which senders you've contacted and when. If something still arrives after a few months, chase that sender again.

title: Travel sick as a passenger? Seat, food and screen habits that help adults
description: Practical ways to reduce car, coach and sea sickness as an adult: where to sit, what to look at, what to eat, and when to ask a pharmacist.
intro: Travel sickness happens when what your eyes see doesn't match the motion your body feels. Plenty of adults still get it. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: In a car, sit in the front passenger seat; on a coach, near the front; on a boat, in the middle and on a lower deck.
Face forwards, and keep your head still against the headrest.
Look out of the front window at the horizon or a fixed point in the distance.
Avoid reading or looking at your phone. If you must, keep it brief and hold the screen up near eye level.
Closing your eyes, or listening to music or an audiobook, can help.
Eat a light meal before you go, and avoid heavy, greasy food and alcohol.
Open a window or turn on the air for cool, fresh air.

p: A pharmacist can recommend travel sickness medicines and explain when to take them, since many work best taken before the journey. See a GP if sickness is severe, new, or comes with other symptoms.
Note each trip: seat, vehicle, what you were doing and how soon you felt sick. After a few trips you'll know what helps you most.

title: No one to look after your dog when you go away? Your options compared
description: Kennels, home boarders, house-sitters, paid sitters and swapping with other owners: costs, what to check, and how to settle a nervous dog.
intro: Leaving a dog is one of the main reasons people skip holidays. There are more options than kennels, and a little planning makes any of them easier on you and your dog.

list: Boarding kennels: licensed, with staff on site. Visit first and ask about exercise, staff numbers and vet cover.
Home boarding: your dog stays in someone's home. Check they're licensed by your local council (in England, home boarders need a licence).
House-sitters: someone stays in your home, often through a membership site.
Paid dog-sitters or walkers who visit, for short trips.
Swapping with other dog owners you know and trust.
Licence or membership, insurance, references and reviews.
Where your dog sleeps, how often it's walked, and who has it if something goes wrong.
Vaccinations: many kennels and boarders require them, including kennel cough.

p: Book a short trial stay or a day visit before your holiday, especially for a nervous or rescue dog.

list: Food amounts and times, walk routine, quirks and fears, and any medication instructions from your vet.
Your vet's details, an emergency contact, and how to reach you.

p: Ask for a daily photo or message. Knowing your dog is fine lets you enjoy the trip.

title: Parents not replying to your child's party invite? How to get a headcount
description: Simple ways to get replies to class party invites: clear deadlines, easy ways to reply, polite reminders, and planning around a venue's minimum numbers.
intro: Chasing replies is one of the most stressful parts of a class party, especially when you're paying per head. A few small changes get far more replies.

list: Put a clear reply-by date on the invite, at least a week before the venue's deadline.
Give more than one way to reply: a phone number, an email address and a link or QR code.
Include the time, the place, and whether parents need to stay.
Send one friendly reminder a few days before the deadline, through the class group, the school bag or the teacher if allowed.
Keep a list of who has replied, so you only chase the ones who haven't.
Check the venue's minimum numbers, final-numbers date and payment terms before sending invites.
Assume a few children won't come, even if their parents said yes.

p: Have a list of who said yes for the door, and a couple of spare party bags for late additions.

title: Are my solar panels working properly? How to check without climbing on the roof
description: Simple checks from the ground: read your generation meter, compare with what your system should make, watch for zero days, and know when to call an installer.
intro: Solar panels can underperform for months before anyone notices. A few minutes a week with your meter or app will tell you. Never go on the roof or open electrical equipment; call an accredited installer for faults.

list: Find your generation meter (often near the inverter or consumer unit) and note the total once a week on the same day.
The difference between readings is what your panels made that week.

sections.h: Compare with what it should make
list: Your installation paperwork usually includes an estimate of yearly generation; divide by 12 for a rough monthly figure, remembering summer is much higher than winter.
Compare with the same month last year. A big drop in similar weather is worth investigating.
Look at the inverter's display or lights. A red or orange light or an error code often means it has stopped. Note the code and check the manual.
A zero day in good weather usually means the inverter or a connection has a problem.
Inverter faults, which are the most common cause of a sudden stop.
New shading from trees or buildings, or heavy dirt in areas with little rain.
A tripped isolator or breaker. Only reset what the manual says is safe; otherwise call an installer.

p: Contact your installer or an accredited installer (MCS-certified in the UK). Keep your weekly readings, since they help with warranty claims.

title: Worried you have bad breath? How to tell, and what usually helps
description: Simple ways to check your own breath, the everyday causes, a routine that helps most people, and when to see a dentist or GP.
intro: Most bad breath starts in the mouth and improves with a good routine. It's hard to judge your own breath, so a few simple checks and notes help. This is general information, not dental or medical advice.

list: Lick the inside of your wrist, let it dry for a few seconds, then smell it.
Gently scrape the back of your tongue with a clean spoon and smell it.
Ask one trusted person to tell you honestly.
Food and bacteria left on teeth, gums and the tongue.
Dry mouth, which can come from not drinking enough water, breathing through your mouth, or some medicines.
Strong foods (garlic, onions, spices), coffee, alcohol and smoking.
Gum disease or other dental problems.
Brush twice a day for two minutes, and clean between your teeth once a day.
Clean your tongue gently, from back to front.
Drink water through the day, and chew sugar-free gum after meals.
See a dentist and hygienist regularly.

p: See a dentist if it doesn't improve with a good routine, or if your gums bleed or are sore. See a GP if your dentist finds no cause in your mouth.
For two weeks, note days that seemed worse and what came before: food, drink, sleep, a cold or stress. It helps you and your dentist spot the cause.

title: Scared of lifts? Small steps that help many people with claustrophobia
description: How gradual practice works for a fear of lifts and small spaces, a simple step ladder, calming techniques, and when to get professional help.
intro: A fear of lifts is common, and avoiding them usually makes the fear stronger over time. Many people improve with gradual, repeated practice. This is general information, not therapy; if your fear is severe or causes panic attacks, talk to a GP.

p: You start with a step that makes you a little uneasy, stay with it until the unease drops, and repeat it before moving to the next step. Over time your body learns the situation is safe.

list: Watch a lift open and close from a distance.
Stand by the open doors, then step in and out while someone holds them.
Ride one floor with someone you trust, then one floor alone.
Ride several floors, then at a busier time.
Slow breathing: breathe in for 4, out for 6, for a minute or two.
Notice what you can see and hear, and remind yourself the feeling will pass.
Rate your unease from 0 to 10 before and after; seeing it fall helps.

p: Only practise in normal, working public lifts. Never force doors or use a lift that's out of order.

sections.h: Get help if you need it
p: CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) is an effective treatment for phobias. In the UK you can often refer yourself to NHS talking therapies, or ask your GP.

title: How to remember your pelvic floor exercises every day (discreetly)
description: Tie your sets to things you already do, use reminders nobody else can read, and keep track so the routine your physio set actually happens.
intro: Most people know they should do pelvic floor exercises but forget. Linking them to daily habits works better than willpower. This is general information; follow the routine your physio, GP or NHS leaflet gives you.

sections.h: Follow the routine you were given
p: The NHS suggests building up to at least 3 sets of 8 squeezes each day, but follow what your physio or GP advises for you. Pelvic floor exercises aren't right for everyone, so get checked if you have pain or your symptoms don't improve.

list: While the kettle boils, while you brush your teeth, at red lights, during feeds, or in an advert break.
Choose three moments you never miss, and use the same ones every day.
Name the reminder something only you understand, and turn off alert previews.
Vibration-only reminders are easy to ignore in public, but nobody else will notice them.

p: Tick off each set, including ones you do away from your phone. A weekly tally shows whether the routine is really happening, and is useful at physio appointments.
If you still leak or have heaviness or pain after a few months of regular exercises, ask your GP to refer you to a pelvic health physiotherapist.

title: How to find your eczema triggers with a two-week diary
description: Common eczema triggers, a simple daily diary, testing one change at a time, and when to see a GP or pharmacist.
intro: Eczema triggers vary from person to person, which is why advice often conflicts. A short, consistent diary helps you see your own pattern. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Irritants: soaps, shower gels, washing-up liquid, detergents and frequent hand washing.
Weather: cold, dry air, heat and sweating.
Fabrics such as wool and some synthetics.
Stress, and for some people dust mites, pets, pollen or certain foods.
How your skin is (calm, itchy or flaring) and where.
What you washed with, any new products, the weather, stress, sleep and anything unusual.
Which creams you used and when.

sections.h: Test one change at a time
p: After two weeks, pick one likely trigger, such as a new shower gel, and change only that for two weeks. Changing several things at once makes it impossible to tell what helped.
Take a photo of the same patch, in the same light and angle, every few days. It's easier to see real change than to rely on memory.

Talk to a pharmacist or GP if your eczema isn't improving, is affecting sleep or daily life, or you're unsure about treatments. Get urgent help if skin is hot, swollen, weeping or crusted, or you feel unwell.

title: Learning to lip read with hearing loss: how to start at home
description: What lipreading can and can't do, how to practise at home, tips for everyday conversations, and where to find classes.
intro: Lipreading won't catch every word, because many sounds look the same on the lips. But combined with hearing aids, context and good conditions, it can make conversations much easier. This is general information, not medical advice.

p: If your hearing has dropped suddenly, get medical help urgently. For gradual changes, see a GP or audiologist; hearing aids and lipreading work well together.

list: Watching lip shapes, the jaw, the tongue and facial expressions.
Using the topic and key words to fill in gaps; context does a lot of the work.
Many sounds look alike (for example p, b and m), so expect to guess and check.
Watch TV or videos with subtitles, then try a short clip with the sound low and subtitles off.
Practise with a patient friend or relative: start with single words on a known topic, then short sentences.
Little and often (10 to 15 minutes a day) works better than long sessions.
Sit facing the light, with the speaker's face well lit and not in shadow.
Ask people to face you, not cover their mouth, and speak clearly without exaggerating.
Choose quieter places, and tell people what helps you.

p: Lipreading classes are run by some councils, adult education services and hearing loss charities. Ask your audiologist or search for local classes; some are online.

title: How to help your child learn their weekly spellings (without nightly battles)
description: Short, daily practice that focuses on the words your child gets wrong, simple techniques that work better than copying, and how to keep it calm.
intro: Copying words out over and over is one of the least effective ways to learn spellings. Short, varied practice focused on the tricky words works better and causes fewer battles.

p: Five minutes a day beats one long session the night before the test. Pick a regular time, such as after a snack.

sections.h: Test first, then practise the misses
list: Start each session with a quick test of the list.
Only practise the words they got wrong, and leave the ones they know.

sections.h: Techniques that work better than copying
list: Look, say, cover, write, check: look at the word, say it, cover it, write it from memory, then check.
Spot the tricky part of the word and say it in an exaggerated way (for example 'Wed-nes-day').
Make up a silly sentence or picture for a hard word.
Praise effort, not just right answers.
Stop on a success, and keep sessions short so they don't become a fight.
Mix last week's tricky words back in now and then.

p: Do one relaxed practice test of the whole list, then stop. A good night's sleep helps more than extra drilling.

title: How to track perimenopause symptoms before a GP appointment
description: What to record, how long for, and how to present it, so a short appointment covers what matters. UK-focused.
intro: Perimenopause symptoms can be varied and come and go, which makes them easy to forget in a ten-minute appointment. A simple record helps. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Changes to periods (more or less often, heavier or lighter).
Hot flushes, night sweats and poor sleep.
Low mood, anxiety, irritability, brain fog and poor concentration.
Aches, headaches, tiredness, vaginal dryness and lower sex drive.
Each day: which symptoms, how bad (0 to 3), and when your period started and stopped.
The impact: missed sleep, time off work, things you've stopped doing.
Anything you've tried and whether it helped.

p: Two to three months gives a clear picture, but even a few weeks is useful. Don't wait to book if symptoms are affecting your life.

list: Bring a one-page summary: main symptoms, how often, how long, and the impact.
Write down your questions first, and say what you'd like to discuss.
In the UK, NICE guidance says women over 45 with typical symptoms can usually be diagnosed without a blood test.
Bleeding is very heavy or unusual, or happens after sex, between periods or after your periods have stopped.
You have thoughts of self-harm, or symptoms that worry you.

title: How to keep a migraine diary that actually finds your triggers
description: What to record for each attack and each day, how long to keep it, how to spot patterns, and what to take to your GP.
intro: Migraine triggers are personal and often combine, which makes them hard to spot from memory. A simple diary kept for a few weeks shows much more. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: You have a sudden, very severe headache unlike any before.
A headache comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness, numbness, slurred speech or vision loss, or follows a head injury.
When it started and ended, how bad it was (0 to 3), and where the pain was.
Any aura or warning signs, and what you took and whether it helped.
Sleep, meals (including skipped ones), caffeine, alcohol and water.
Stress, screen time, exercise, and where you are in your cycle if relevant.
Weather changes you notice.

p: After four to eight weeks, compare the 24 hours before attacks with clear days. Triggers often combine, such as poor sleep plus a skipped meal.

Count the days each month you take painkillers. Taking them on many days can itself cause more headaches, so mention it to your GP or pharmacist. Take your diary to appointments; it helps a doctor see frequency and patterns quickly.

title: The Schengen 90/180-day rule explained, with a simple way to count your days
description: How the rolling 180-day window works, why simple calendar counting goes wrong, and how to plan your next trip safely. Not legal advice.
intro: Visitors on many non-EU passports, including UK passports, can stay in the Schengen area for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. The rolling window is what confuses most people. This is general information, not legal or immigration advice; check the official rules for your passport.

list: On any given day, look back over the previous 180 days (including today).
Count every day you were in the Schengen area in that window. The total must be 90 or less.
Days in any Schengen country all count together, and your entry and exit days both count as days in.
It isn't 90 days per half-year or per calendar year: the window moves forward every day.
Days 'come back' only when they drop out of the back of the 180-day window.
Before booking, check how many days you'll have on the planned entry date and on each day of the trip.
Use the EU's official short-stay calculator to check your plan.

p: Residence permits, long-stay visas, family members of EU citizens and some national arrangements can change what applies to you. Check which countries are in the Schengen area, and get official advice if your situation is unusual.
Keep a list of every entry and exit date, and boarding passes or tickets, in case you're asked at the border.

title: How to keep a heartburn and reflux diary that shows your triggers
description: Common reflux triggers, what to log for meals and flares, everyday changes that help many people, and when to see a GP.
intro: Reflux triggers differ from person to person, and timing matters as much as food. A few weeks of simple notes usually shows a pattern. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: You have chest pain that spreads to your arm, jaw or back, or with breathlessness: get urgent help.
You have trouble swallowing, keep vomiting, have black stools, or lose weight without trying.
You've had heartburn most days for three weeks or more, or remedies aren't helping.
Large or late meals, and lying down soon after eating.
Fatty or spicy food, chocolate, coffee, alcohol, citrus and tomatoes.
Smoking, tight clothing and stress.
What you ate and drank, how much, and when.
Each flare: time, how bad (0 to 3), and what you took.
When you went to bed, and anything else unusual that day.

sections.h: Everyday changes that help many people
list: Eat smaller meals, and leave three to four hours between your last meal and bed.
Raise the head of your bed slightly.
Try changing one thing at a time for two weeks, so you can tell what helped.

p: A pharmacist can advise on remedies. Don't stop or change prescribed medicines without talking to your GP.

title: How to clear a read-later backlog of hundreds of saved articles
description: A guilt-free way to work through saved articles: count it, set a daily round, let most go, and stop the pile growing back.
intro: Most read-later piles grow faster than anyone can read them. The goal isn't to read everything; it's to read the few that matter and let the rest go.

list: Export everything from your read-later app or bookmarks first, so nothing is lost.
Count it and estimate the hours: at five to ten minutes an article, a thousand saves is days of reading.
Anything older than a year that you can't remember saving can usually go.
News and time-sensitive pieces are often out of date; drop them.

p: Take ten items a day. For each: read it now, skim it, keep it for a set time, or let it go. Ten decisions take a few minutes.

list: Before saving, ask whether you'd read it this week.
Give saves an expiry date, so unread ones disappear on their own.
Unsubscribe from newsletters you always save but never read.

p: Keep a short list of the pieces that were genuinely worth it, and revisit them. That small list is the real value of reading later.

title: Coaching your child's team for the first time: a simple practice plan
description: How to structure a practice for young children, games that keep everyone moving, and how to avoid running out of ideas mid-season.
intro: Young children learn best through short, active games, not lines and lectures. A simple, repeatable structure takes most of the stress out of volunteer coaching.

list: Warm-up game (5-10 minutes) that gets everyone moving straight away.
One skill game (10-15 minutes), such as dribbling, throwing or catching.
A small-sided game (10-15 minutes) with lots of touches for everyone.
A short cool-down and a high five for each child.
Avoid lines: give every child a ball where you can.
Explain in under 30 seconds, then let them play; correct as you go.
Small teams (3 vs 3, 4 vs 4) mean more turns for everyone.

p: Pick one theme a week and build on it, repeating favourite games. Children love repetition, and you don't need new ideas every week.
Ask one or two parents to run a station or a small game. Give them a clear, simple job.
Follow your league's safeguarding and background-check rules, keep water and first-aid nearby, and never be alone with one child.

title: How to keep a restless legs diary that shows what makes nights worse
description: What to note each evening and morning, how to spot patterns over three weeks, and what to tell your GP. Not medical advice.
intro: Restless legs often vary from night to night, which makes patterns hard to see from memory. A short, easy diary helps you and your GP. This is general information, not medical advice.

p: If restless legs are affecting your sleep, talk to a GP. They may check for things that can make it worse, such as low iron levels, and review any medicines you take. Don't change prescribed medicines without advice.

list: Caffeine (including tea, cola and chocolate), alcohol and smoking.
Late or heavy meals, long periods of sitting, exercise, a hot bath and stress.
Anything new you've started taking.
How bad it was (0 to 3), how long it kept you awake, and whether you had to get up and walk.
Anything that helped, such as stretching, walking or massage.

p: One tap in the morning and a few in the evening is enough. A diary you can keep up for three weeks beats a detailed one you abandon after three days.
After three weeks, compare the evenings before bad nights with the ones before calmer nights, then try changing one thing at a time for two weeks.

title: How to teach yourself shorthand (Gregg or Teeline) and build speed
description: Choosing a system, a simple daily routine, how to check your outlines, and how to build speed with dictation.
intro: Shorthand can still be learned at home with a manual and steady practice. Little and often, plus dictation, is what builds real speed.

list: Gregg is widely used in the US, with many old manuals freely available.
Teeline is common in the UK, especially in journalism training.
Pick one and stick with it; mixing systems slows you down.
15-20 minutes a day: learn a few new outlines, then review older ones.
Write each new outline several times, saying the word as you write.

p: Compare what you write with the model outlines in your manual. Proportion and direction matter, so check size and angle, not just shape.

list: Once you know the theory, take dictation: start slowly (about 40 words per minute) and raise the speed gradually.
Always read back what you wrote, and note outlines you couldn't read.

p: Record your speed and accuracy each week. Steady gains come from regular short sessions, not occasional long ones.

title: Learning braille as a sighted adult: where to start
description: How braille works, the order to learn it in, writing practice, and where to find support, for parents, partners and trainee teachers.
intro: Many sighted adults learn braille to support a child, partner or friend, or for work. Starting visually and building up step by step makes it far less intimidating.

list: Each braille cell has six dot positions in two columns of three.
Letters, numbers and punctuation are made from different dot patterns.
Unified English Braille (UEB) is the standard used in the UK, the US and many other English-speaking countries.
The alphabet first (letters a to j form the pattern for the rest).
Punctuation and numbers.
Contractions (Grade 2), which shorten common words and letter groups and are used in most books.

p: Braille is often written on a six-key braille writer, with one key per dot. Practising the six-key layout helps you remember the dot patterns.
Once you know the letters, practise reading words and sentences with the print hidden, so you rely on the dots.
Sight-loss charities, schools and qualified teachers of the visually impaired often offer courses and resources for families and learners.

title: Nervous about docking your boat? A calm pre-approach checklist
description: How to plan an approach to your slip, brief your crew in 30 seconds, and practise in open water so docking stops being the part you dread.
intro: Most boaters find docking the hardest part, especially with wind, current or people watching. A plan made before you arrive makes a big difference. This is general information, not boating instruction; take lessons from a qualified instructor.

list: Check the wind and current at your berth, and decide which side you'll come in on.
Rig fenders and lines on the right side before you enter the marina.
Decide your abort plan: where you'll go round again if the approach isn't working.
Who handles the bow line, who handles the stern line, and who fends off.
Tell everyone to step, not jump, onto the dock, and never put hands or feet between the boat and the dock.
Everyone wears a lifejacket.
Go slowly: only as fast as you need for control. Short bursts of power work better than steady throttle.
If it's going wrong, back out and try again; there's no prize for getting it first time.

p: Practise in open water using a buoy or a fender as a target, and practise at quiet times of day. Lessons with an instructor on your own boat are often the quickest way to build confidence.
Afterwards, note the conditions and what went well or wrong. Patterns, such as always drifting one way, tell you exactly what to practise.

title: Using airline points for a family holiday in school holidays: how to find the seats
description: Why reward seats for four or five people are hard to find, when seats are released, and practical ways to get the whole family on a flight.
intro: Reward seats are limited, and school-holiday dates are the most popular of all. Planning around release dates and staying flexible on the details gives you the best chance.

p: Many airlines release reward seats around a year before departure, and the exact day varies by airline. Check your programme's rules and set a reminder for the release day of your outbound and return dates.

list: Consider nearby airports, different days within the holiday, or flying out and back on different routes.
Look at partner airlines in the same alliance.
If only two seats appear, book two and keep looking; more often appear later, or try back-to-back flights.
Mixing cabins (some in economy, some premium) can work on long flights.

p: Compare the points plus taxes and fees with the cash fare. On some routes the fees are high, and paying cash and saving points is better value.
Seat-alert tools can notify you when seats appear, so you don't have to search every day.

title: Wedding planning when you don't know where to start: the first five decisions
description: The handful of decisions that unlock everything else, how to split a budget by what you care about, and how to stop feeling overwhelmed.
intro: Wedding planning feels huge because everything seems urgent at once. In reality, a few early decisions shape all the rest, and most things can wait.

list: Your total budget, and who is contributing.
Roughly how many guests.
The season or rough date.
Your top three priorities (for example food, photos and music).
The general area or type of venue.
Put more of the budget into your top three priorities, and less into the things you care least about.
Keep a buffer of around 10% for surprises.
Update the budget as real quotes come in.

p: Venue and date usually come first, then the suppliers who get booked up early in your area. Everything else can follow later.

sections.h: Take it a few steps at a time
p: Choose two or three tasks a week and ignore the rest until next week. A long checklist is useful to keep, but not to look at every day.
Decide together who handles what, and keep one shared list so nothing gets lost in messages.

title: Overpay your mortgage or save? How to compare, and avoid early repayment charges (UK)
description: How to compare your mortgage rate with savings after tax, check your penalty-free overpayment allowance, and plan around the end of a fixed deal. Not advice.
intro: Overpaying a mortgage can save a lot of interest, but it isn't always the best use of spare money. A few numbers make the comparison clearer. This is general information, not financial advice.

list: Overpaying saves you roughly your mortgage interest rate on the amount you overpay.
Saving earns the savings rate, minus any tax on the interest.
If your mortgage rate is higher than what you'd earn after tax, overpaying usually saves more; if it's lower, saving may come out ahead.
Many lenders let you overpay up to a set amount each year (often 10% of the balance) without an early repayment charge during a fixed or discounted deal. Check your own lender's terms.
Overpaying more than the allowance during a deal can trigger a charge.

p: Once you overpay, it's usually hard to get the money back. Keep an emergency fund in easy-access savings first.
When a fix ends you can usually pay off a larger lump sum without a charge. Some people save during the fix and pay down the balance at remortgage, which can also help with the rate you get.
Ask your lender whether overpayments shorten your term or reduce your monthly payment, and choose what suits you.

title: How to find your rosacea triggers: a three-week diary
description: Common rosacea triggers, what to log each day, how to test one change at a time, and when to see a GP or dermatologist.
intro: Rosacea triggers vary from person to person, so general lists only go so far. A short daily diary helps you find your own. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Sun, heat, cold and wind.
Hot drinks, spicy food and alcohol.
Exercise, stress and hot baths or showers.
Some skincare and make-up products.
How your face looked and felt (calm, pink, flushed or flaring), and where.
What you ate and drank, the weather, exercise and stress.
Any products you used, especially new ones.

p: Photograph your face in the same light and angle every few days. It's easier to see real change than to rely on memory.

sections.h: Test one change at a time
p: After three weeks, pick the likeliest trigger and change only that for two weeks. Changing several things at once makes it impossible to tell what helped.
See a GP or dermatologist if rosacea is affecting your confidence or daily life, or if treatments aren't working. Get help promptly if your eyes are sore, gritty or red.

title: Homemade pizza dough tearing or a soggy base? Common causes and fixes
description: Why pizza dough tears or springs back, why bases stay soggy in a home oven, and simple changes to try one at a time.
intro: Most homemade pizza problems come down to the dough's rest and temperature, and how hot the base gets. Change one thing at a time so you know what fixed it.

sections.h: Dough that tears or springs back
list: Let it rest: dough that fights back usually needs 10-20 more minutes covered, so the gluten relaxes.
Let cold dough come up to room temperature before stretching.
Stretch gently from the edges with your knuckles, rather than pulling hard or rolling thin spots.

p: A slightly wetter dough is easier to stretch. Add water a little at a time, and knead or rest until it's smooth.

sections.h: Soggy or raw in the middle
list: Heat your oven as hot as it goes and preheat the tray, stone or steel well before baking.
Bake on a low shelf, close to the heat.
Use less sauce and fewer wet toppings, and stretch the base evenly so the middle isn't thicker.

p: Move the pizza higher in the oven, or switch to the grill for the last minute to finish the top.
Write down your flour, water, proving time, oven temperature and what went wrong each time. After a few bakes, you'll see which change made the difference.

title: How long will it take to save a house deposit? A simple way to work it out
description: Work out your deposit target, a realistic monthly amount and a target date, allow for rising prices, and keep the plan honest. Not financial advice.
intro: A deposit target can feel impossible when prices move. Putting your own numbers on paper usually makes it clearer, and shows which levers make the biggest difference. This is general information, not financial advice.

list: Pick a realistic price range for the area you want.
Decide your deposit percentage (a bigger deposit can mean better mortgage rates), and add costs such as fees, surveys and moving.
Subtract what you've saved from the target, then divide by what you can save each month.
Allow for prices changing: try a few assumptions (for example 0%, 3% and 5% a year) rather than one.
Saving a little more each month, a cheaper area or property type, or a slightly smaller deposit can each move the date a lot.
Look into government schemes or tax-free accounts for first-time buyers that you may be eligible for, and check their rules and limits.

p: Check in once a month: update what you've saved and whether you hit your amount. Missed months are normal; the date just moves.
When you're getting close, a mortgage broker can tell you what you could borrow and what deposit you really need.

title: Baby hates tummy time? Gentle ways to make it easier
description: Short sessions, easier positions, the best times to try, and how to keep it safe. For parents of young babies.
intro: Lots of babies cry during tummy time at first. Short, frequent tries in comfortable positions usually work better than long sessions. Always supervise tummy time, only while your baby is awake, and always put your baby to sleep on their back.

list: Try a minute or two, a few times a day, and build up slowly as your baby copes.
Stop before your baby gets really upset, and try again later.
Lying on your chest while you recline, face to face.
Across your lap, with a gentle hand on their back.
On the floor over a rolled towel under their chest, with you down at their level.
When your baby is awake and content, not hungry or very tired.
Not straight after a feed.

p: Get down on the floor face to face, sing, talk, or use a baby-safe mirror or a favourite toy.
Talk to your health visitor or doctor if you're worried about your baby's development, head shape, or if they always turn their head one way.

title: Toddler screams at hair washing? Small steps that make bath time calmer
description: Why hair washing upsets young children, step-by-step practice, simple tricks to try one at a time, and bath safety.
intro: Water on the face and head scares many young children. Making it predictable, and practising in small steps, often helps more than doing it quickly. Never leave a child alone in the bath, even for a moment, and check the water is warm, not hot.

list: Use the same order every time, and count down before the water comes.
Let your child hold a dry flannel over their eyes, or wear a bath visor.
Play with cups and water outside bath time, or pour water on a toy's head first.
Try a wet flannel on the hair, then a little water at the back, then a quick rinse.

sections.h: Try one trick at a time
list: Tipping back while looking at the ceiling, a handheld shower on low, or washing hair on a different night from the bath.
Keep each trick for a few baths before switching, so you can tell what helps.

p: Hair doesn't need washing every bath for most young children. Fewer, calmer washes beat nightly battles.
If your child suddenly starts refusing baths, or it comes with other changes, talk to your health visitor or doctor.

title: Why is my hay fever worse on some days? A simple two-week diary
description: Everyday steps that reduce pollen exposure, what to note each day, and what to tell a pharmacist or GP when treatments aren't working.
intro: Hay fever often varies from day to day with pollen, weather and what you were doing. A short diary helps you see your own pattern. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Check the pollen forecast, and plan time outdoors for lower-count times where you can.
Shower and change clothes after being outside, and keep windows closed on high-pollen days.
Wear wraparound sunglasses, and avoid drying washing outside when the count is high.
Eyes, nose, throat and sleep, scored 0 to 3.
What you took, and when.
Time outside, cut grass, windows open, exercise and the weather.

p: After two weeks, compare the bad days with the better ones. Timing of medicines, time outdoors and weather often explain a lot.
A pharmacist can suggest different antihistamines, nasal sprays or eye drops, and how and when to use them. Bring your diary.

list: Nothing from the pharmacy helps.
You have wheezing, tightness in the chest or breathing problems.

title: Changing your name after marriage: a checklist and the order to do it in
description: Who to tell, what to do first, which documents to have ready, and how to avoid travel problems. UK-focused, with notes for elsewhere.
intro: Changing your name means telling a lot of organisations, and doing it in a sensible order saves time. This is general information; check each organisation's current rules.

list: Your marriage or civil partnership certificate is usually the proof you need.
Order a few extra certified copies; many places want to see an original or certified copy, not a photocopy.
Photo ID first (driving licence or passport), since banks and others may ask for ID in your new name.
Then banks, credit cards and payroll at work.
Then tax, pensions, insurance, utilities, your mortgage or tenancy, your doctor and dentist, and the electoral register.

p: Your ticket name must match the passport you travel on. If you have a trip booked soon after the wedding, book it in the name on your current passport, or check whether you can apply for a new-name passport before the wedding.

list: Online accounts, loyalty cards, subscriptions, memberships and the vet.
Professional bodies and qualifications.

p: Keep one list and tick off each place as it's done. Old-name accounts often turn up months later; add them as you find them.

title: Didn't get the school place you wanted? How to prepare an appeal (England)
description: Waiting lists, deadlines, finding out how places were allocated, what panels consider, and how to present your case. Not legal advice.
intro: If your child wasn't offered a place at a school you wanted, you usually have the right to appeal to an independent panel. Many appeals don't succeed, so it's worth preparing carefully and keeping other options open. This is general information, not legal advice.

list: Accept the place you've been offered while you appeal, so your child has a school.
Ask to go on the waiting list for every school you'd accept; places can come up.
Note the appeal deadline in your offer letter or on the admission authority's website.

sections.h: Find out how places were given
p: Ask the admission authority how the admission criteria were applied, how distance was measured, and where your child ranked. Mistakes do sometimes happen.

list: Whether the admission arrangements were lawful and applied correctly.
Whether your child's reasons for needing that school outweigh the problems an extra pupil would cause.
Reasons such as childcare or convenience usually carry less weight than specific needs the school can meet.

p: For reception to Year 2, class sizes are limited by law, so grounds for appeal are much narrower.

list: Write clearly and briefly, with evidence for each reason.
Practise answering questions for the hearing, and bring copies of your documents.

title: Period pain and painkillers not working? What to write down before you see your GP
description: How to keep a simple three-cycle record of period pain, what to bring to an appointment, and when to get help.
intro: Severe period pain isn't something you just have to put up with. A clear record helps a GP understand how much it affects you. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Period pain stops you working, studying or doing everyday things.
Painkillers from the pharmacy don't help.
You have pain between periods, during or after sex, or very heavy bleeding.

p: You have sudden, severe pain, you faint, or you're bleeding very heavily.

list: The days with pain, how bad (0-10), and where it hurt.
What you took, when, and whether it helped.
What the pain stopped you doing, and how heavy the bleeding was.
Three cycles of records, summarised on one page.
What you've already tried, and your questions.
Say clearly how it affects your life; that's what helps a doctor decide on next steps.

p: You can ask for a second opinion, or to see a GP with an interest in women's health. A clear written record makes it easier to explain.

title: Builder left the job unfinished or stopped answering? What to do next (UK)
description: How to record what's been paid and done, chase in writing, set a final deadline, and where to go for help. Not legal advice.
intro: When a builder stops turning up partway through a job, a clear written record and a calm paper trail give you the most options. This is general information, not legal advice; Citizens Advice can help with your situation.

list: What was agreed (quotes, messages, any contract), what you've paid and when, and what's been done.
Dated photos of the work as it stands.
Every call, message and promise, with dates.

p: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, a trader must carry out a service with reasonable care and skill, and within a reasonable time if no date was agreed. If they don't, you may be entitled to have it put right or to a price reduction.

list: Send a clear message asking them to return and finish by a specific date.
If nothing happens, send a final letter giving a last deadline and saying what you'll do next, such as bringing in another trader or making a claim.
If you paid by credit card, you may be able to claim from the card provider (purchases between £100 and £30,000).
If the trader is a member of a trade body, it may have a dispute scheme.
Small claims are possible for smaller amounts, but a judgment isn't always collectable.

p: Contact the Citizens Advice consumer helpline, which can refer cases to Trading Standards. Don't stop paying for or start another trader on unsafe electrical, gas or structural work without professional advice.

title: How to record a week of home blood pressure readings for your GP
description: A calm, consistent way to take and write down home blood pressure readings when your GP or nurse asks for a week of them. A record, not medical advice.
intro: If your GP or nurse has asked you to check your blood pressure at home, the most useful thing you can hand back is a consistent record. Always follow the instructions you were given and the leaflet that came with your monitor; this guide is about keeping the record, not about what the numbers mean.

list: Avoid caffeine, smoking and exercise for about 30 minutes beforehand, if your instructions say so.
Empty your bladder, then sit quietly for about 5 minutes with your back supported and feet flat on the floor.
Rest your arm on a table at about chest height, with the cuff on bare skin, and don't talk during the reading.
Take the number of readings you were asked for, usually 2, about a minute apart.
Do it at the same times each day, often once in the morning and once in the evening.
Use the same arm each time, unless you were told otherwise.
The date and time, and every reading (top number, bottom number and pulse), not just the lowest.
A short note on anything unusual: a bad night, rushing, pain, feeling anxious, or a missed dose.
Keep going for the number of days you were asked, even if some readings look odd.

p: It's common for readings taken minutes apart to differ, and many people read higher at the surgery than at home. Write every reading down and let your GP or nurse look at the pattern. Don't change any medication on the strength of home readings unless your GP tells you to.

If you get a very high reading and also have symptoms such as chest pain, a severe headache, breathlessness, weakness, confusion or changes in your vision, call 999. If you're worried about your readings, contact your GP or NHS 111.

title: Child can read but won't read for fun? Gentle ways to find the book that clicks
description: Practical, low-pressure ideas for parents of 7-12 year olds who can read but avoid books.
intro: Plenty of children who read perfectly well still say books are boring. Pressure usually makes it worse; matching books to what they already love, and keeping reading time relaxed, tends to work better. This is about reading for pleasure; if you're worried about how your child is learning to read, talk to their teacher.

list: Write down their three biggest interests right now: a game, a sport, an animal, a YouTuber, a joke style.
Look for books on exactly those things, including non-fiction, joke books, annuals and game guides.
Ask a children's librarian for 'books like' a film or game they enjoy.
Comics, graphic novels and illustrated chapter books are real reading.
Short books and series with short chapters give quick wins.
Audiobooks alongside the printed book can help a child stay with a story.
Read aloud to them, even if they can read alone; take turns page by page.
Stop on a cliffhanger, not when they're bored.
Let them drop a book they don't like, and note it so you choose better next time.

p: Points and prizes can make reading feel like a job. Keeping a simple private note of what they finished and what they dropped helps you spot the kind of book that actually holds their attention.

title: School morning routine without the shouting: a calmer way out of the door
description: How to find the step that stalls your school morning and plan a routine your 4-10 year old can follow.
intro: If every school morning ends in nagging and a dash for the door, the problem is often one or two steps that eat the time. A little planning the night before and a routine your child can see usually helps more than more reminders.

list: Write down when you must leave the house.
Count back the minutes each step really takes: waking, dressing, breakfast, teeth, shoes and coats.
Add five spare minutes, and set the wake-up time from there.
For a week, note which step made you late each morning.
Shoes, breakfast and screens are common culprits.
Change one thing at a time, such as shoes and coats by the door the night before.

sections.h: Let a picture list do the reminding
list: Make a simple picture checklist your child can follow in order.
Give each step a timer so the clock, not you, says it's time to move on.
Keep the same order every day.

sections.h: Do the rest the night before
list: Lay out clothes and pack bags in the evening.
Agree screens stay off until everyone is ready, if that helps your family.
Keep a calm 'leave now' cue so the last minutes aren't a scramble.

title: How to keep track of oil changes and car services (and a service history that helps when you sell)
description: A simple way to set maintenance reminders from your owner's manual and keep records you'll actually use.
intro: Most people don't forget car maintenance because they don't care; they forget because the reminder lives in a glovebox sticker or a garage's memory. A few minutes setting up from your owner's manual, and a quick monthly mileage check, is usually enough. This is general information, not mechanical advice.

list: Look in your owner's manual or service book for the oil change and service intervals.
Note both the mileage and the time limit (for example, every so many miles or every 12 months, whichever comes first).
If you mostly do short trips, tow or drive in dusty conditions, check whether the manual lists a 'severe' schedule.

sections.h: Check your mileage once a month
list: Pick a fixed day, such as the first of the month, and note the odometer reading.
Compare it with when the next oil change or service is due.
Book the next job when you're within a month or about 1,000 miles of it.
Write down the date, mileage, what was done, who did it and the cost.
Keep receipts, a photo is fine, with the matching entry.
Include the small things: tyres, wipers, bulbs and battery.

sections.h: Make it useful when you sell
p: A tidy, dated service history with receipts shows a buyer the car has been looked after. Keep the records together in date order, for every car you own, so you can print or share them in one go.
If a warning light comes on, or the car feels, sounds or smells wrong, don't wait for the next service: have it checked by a qualified mechanic.

title: Horse won't load into the trailer? Calm steps to try (and when to get help)
description: A safe, force-free way to approach trailer loading: check the trailer, practise in small steps, and know when to call a vet or trainer.
intro: A horse that won't load is stressful, especially on show or vet day. Pressure and force tend to make it worse and can get people and horses hurt. This is general information; for a horse that is dangerous to load, work with an experienced trainer.

list: Wear a hat, gloves and sturdy boots, and have a helper.
Never stand directly behind the horse or in the path of a horse that might rush back out.
Stop if either of you is getting upset, and finish on a calm moment.
Look at the floor and ramp for soft spots, gaps or slipperiness.
Check for wasps, sharp edges and anything rattling or loose.
Make it light and open inside: open the front, move the divider across if you can.

sections.h: Practise when you don't need to go anywhere
list: Break loading into small steps: walking past, standing at the ramp, one foot on, front feet on, all the way in.
Reward each small step and stop while it's going well.
Note how far you got each time, so you can see progress across sessions.

sections.h: If he used to load fine
p: A sudden change can have a physical cause, such as pain, so talk to your vet. Think about what changed: a new trailer, a scary journey, a different driver or a new yard.
If your horse rears, pulls back hard or rushes out, get help from a qualified trainer rather than trying harder on your own.

title: Hard-to-catch horse? A calmer way to catch him in the field
description: Low-pressure ways to make catching easier, with no chasing, and how to spot what makes it harder.
intro: Spending an hour walking round a field with a halter is maddening, and it often gets worse when catching always means work. A calmer routine usually helps. This is general information; if your horse is aggressive in the field, get help from a qualified trainer.

list: Chasing teaches a horse that people mean running. It can also get you or the horse hurt.
Walk calmly, slightly to the side of his shoulder rather than straight at his face.
If he walks away, stop, wait and try again in a moment.
Sometimes catch him, give a scratch or a small treat and let him go again.
Don't make every catch end in riding or something he dislikes.
Catch him at different times of day, not only when work is coming.
Practise in a small pen or yard first, then a smaller paddock, then the open field.
Be careful around other horses, which can crowd you or kick.

p: Write down how long each catch took, the time of day, who else was in the field and what followed. Patterns often show up within a week or two.
If a horse that was easy to catch suddenly isn't, pain can be a reason, so talk to your vet. If he turns towards you, kicks or bites, ask a qualified trainer for help.

title: How to stop losing your temper behind the wheel
description: Practical ways to stay calmer with other drivers: spot your triggers, plan ahead and let it go before it ruins your day.
intro: Lots of people who are calm everywhere else get angry in traffic. Anger on the road makes driving riskier and spoils the rest of the day. These are general habits that help; if your anger has led to threats or violence, talk to your GP or a qualified professional.

list: After a drive, once you're parked, jot down what set you off: tailgating, slow drivers, being cut up, close passes.
Note the route and time of day; running late is one of the most common triggers.
After a week or two, look for the one or two situations that come up most.
Leave a few minutes earlier so lateness isn't adding to the pressure.
Pick a route or time that avoids your worst trigger where you can.
Decide in advance what you'll do when it happens: breathe out slowly, ease off, let them go.
Keep a bigger gap to the car in front so you have room and time.
Don't gesture, flash, chase or brake-check; it can escalate quickly.
Remind yourself you don't know why the other driver did it, and it isn't personal.

sections.h: If someone is aggressive towards you
p: Don't engage. Keep your doors locked, don't get out of the car, and if you feel in danger drive to a busy public place and call 999.
Take a minute before you go into the house or office. A quick note of what happened, and what you'd do differently, helps the next drive go better.

title: Nightmares every night as an adult: what to note down and when to see a GP
description: A calm way to keep track of frequent or recurring nightmares, the things worth noticing, and when to get help. Not medical advice.
intro: Most adults have a bad dream now and then, but nightmares most nights can wear you down. Keeping a short, simple record can help you and your GP see what's going on. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Nightmares happen most nights or are affecting your mood, work or relationships.
They started after a new medicine or a change of dose. Don't stop a medicine without talking to your GP first.
They follow something traumatic, or come with loud snoring, gasping or pauses in breathing at night.
Whether you had a bad dream, and how upsetting it was on a 0-10 scale.
Whether it woke you, and whether you got back to sleep.
You don't need to write down what happened in it.
Late meals, alcohol and caffeine.
Screens or frightening films close to bedtime.
Stress, poor sleep or a change of routine.
Any new medicine.
Keep a regular bedtime and wake time.
Give yourself 30 minutes of something calm before bed.
If you wake from a nightmare, sit up, put a light on, breathe slowly and remind yourself where you are before trying to sleep again.

p: Some people find it helps to rewrite a recurring bad dream with a different, calmer ending during the day, and read it over before bed. Keep it short, skip the frightening details, and stop if it makes you feel worse. A GP or therapist can guide you through approaches like this properly.

title: How to cut down nuisance and spam calls (UK and US)
description: Free steps to reduce unwanted sales and spam calls, how to opt out, and where to complain.
intro: Blocking numbers one by one rarely keeps up, because callers switch numbers. A few free steps, plus a simple record of who calls, usually works better. This is general information.

list: UK: register your landline and mobile with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS). It's free and can take up to 28 days to take full effect.
US: add your numbers to the National Do Not Call Registry at donotcall.gov. It's free.

sections.h: When a nuisance call comes in
list: Don't press any buttons or say 'yes'; just hang up.
Never give personal or bank details to a caller you didn't expect, even if they say they're from your bank.
Note the number, time, company name and what they said.
If a company you've dealt with keeps calling, ask it in writing to stop calling and to stop using your details for marketing.
Check the marketing settings with companies you've bought from, and untick sharing with 'partners'.
UK: report unwanted marketing calls and texts to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). Report scam texts by forwarding them to 7726.
US: report unwanted calls to the FTC at donotcall.gov or reportfraud.ftc.gov.
A dated log of calls makes a complaint much stronger.

p: Most phones and networks offer free spam filtering or a setting to silence unknown callers. For landlines, some phones and adapters can screen calls.

title: Lower back keeps going out every few months? What to note down for your GP or physio
description: A simple way to track back flare-ups and what comes before them, plus the symptoms that need urgent help. Not medical advice.
intro: If your lower back 'goes' every few months, it can feel random. A short, regular note of what you did before each flare-up often helps you and your GP or physio spot a pattern. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: You have numbness around your bottom or genitals, or can't control your bladder or bowels: call 999 or go to A&E.
You have weakness or numbness in both legs, a high temperature, or the pain started after a fall or accident.
Contact your GP if the pain isn't easing after a few weeks, or keeps coming back.
Your pain on a 0-10 scale.
How long you sat, drove or stood still today.
Any lifting, gardening, exercise or long journeys.
What you were doing just before, and what you'd done the day before.
How many days it took to settle.
What helped, such as gentle movement, heat or rest.
Long periods of sitting, and the chair or car seat you use.
A new mattress, a new bike setup or new shoes.
Poor sleep and stress.

p: If a physio has given you exercises, tick them off when you do them. After a month or two you can see whether the flare-ups change, which is useful to tell your physio. Don't start new exercises during a flare without advice.

title: No Global Entry interview appointments? How to find an earlier slot before your trip
description: Practical ways to get a Global Entry interview sooner after conditional approval. Independent guide, not affiliated with CBP.
intro: After conditional approval, many people find their nearest enrollment centre booked for months. Slots do open up when others cancel or reschedule, and there are other routes. This is an independent guide; always check the official Trusted Traveler Programs website for current rules.

sections.h: Check more often, and more widely
list: Cancellations appear without notice, often a few days ahead, so check regularly.
Look at every centre you could reasonably reach, not just the nearest.
If you book a later slot now, you can usually still reschedule to an earlier one if it opens.
Many US airports let conditionally approved applicants finish the interview when they arrive back from an international trip, with no appointment.
Check the official list of participating airports before you fly, and bring the documents the official site asks for.
Each person needs their own interview.
Look for slots close together at the same centre, or use Enrollment on Arrival when you travel together.

p: Conditional approval doesn't last for ever. Check your official account for the deadline to complete your interview, and set a reminder well before it.
Only book on the official government site. Program fees are paid to the government only. Be wary of websites that charge to 'process' your application.

title: Why am I not catching any fish? A checklist for new anglers
description: Blanked again? Work through spot, timing, bait, rig and bite detection in order, and change one thing at a time.
intro: Every angler blanks, but trip after trip without a fish usually means one or two things are off. Going through them in order, and changing one at a time, is the quickest way to find out which. Always check local licence rules and size limits first.

sections.h: 1. Are there fish where you are?
list: Ask the local tackle shop or club what's being caught, where and on what.
Watch other anglers: if nobody is catching, it may be the day, not you.
Look for features fish like: drop-offs, weed beds, rocks, current seams and structure.
At sea, many spots fish best around certain states of the tide; ask locally which.
Dawn and dusk are often better than the middle of a bright day.
Season matters: some species move in and out through the year.
Use the bait the locals use, as fresh as you can get.
Make sure your hook size suits the fish you're after.
Try different depths, from close in to further out, before moving spot.
Watch your rod tip or float closely, and keep your line fairly tight.
Count bites as well as fish; bites with no fish point to hook size or timing of the strike.

p: Write down the spot, time, tide or flow, weather, bait and rig each trip, and change only one thing next time. After a few trips you'll see what came with bites.
Check tide times, keep away from slippery rocks and fast water, wear sensible footwear, and tell someone where you're going.

title: How to check your payslip against the hours you worked
description: A simple way for hourly and shift workers to spot pay mistakes, and what to do if your pay is short. Not legal advice.
intro: Pay mistakes happen more often than people think, especially with shifts, overtime and changing hours. Keeping your own record makes them easy to spot and much easier to sort out. This is general information, not legal or tax advice.

list: Write down when each shift started and finished, and any unpaid breaks.
Note overtime, night or weekend shifts, and holiday taken.
Keep rotas, messages about shift changes and every payslip.
Compare the hours paid with your own record for the same pay period.
Check the hourly rate, including any overtime or shift rates you were promised.
Check deductions you don't recognise, and your tax code (UK).

p: Divide your pay for the period by the hours you worked to get your actual hourly rate, and compare it with the minimum wage for your age and location. Unpaid time you're required to work, such as some training or compulsory tasks, may count.

list: Raise it politely with payroll or your manager in writing, saying which pay period, which hours and what you think is missing.
Keep a copy of what you sent and any reply.
UK: Acas gives free, confidential advice on pay problems, and you can complain to HMRC about minimum wage. US: contact your state labor office or the Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division.

title: Scared of cycling on busy roads? How to build up to a bike commute
description: Practical steps for nervous adult riders: quieter routes, practice at quiet times, and where to get proper cycle training.
intro: Lots of people would like to cycle to work but are put off by traffic. Building up slowly on a route you know, at quiet times, and getting some proper training, helps most riders feel far more in control. This is general information, not cycle training.

list: In the UK, Bikeability training covers riding on roads and junctions, and many councils run adult sessions, sometimes free or low-cost.
Elsewhere, look for local cycle-training or bike-club beginner rides.
A trainer can ride your actual commute with you.
It's fine to take a longer route that uses back streets, paths and cycle lanes.
Ride or walk it first without time pressure and note the junctions that worry you.
For each one, decide where you'll position yourself, or whether to get off and walk across.
Ride the route first on a quiet Sunday morning.
Then try a quiet weekday time, then the real commute.
