Move to the next step only when the last one feels manageable.
Under the Highway Code, you can ride in the centre of the lane on quiet roads, in slower-moving traffic and at the approach to junctions, to make yourself seen.
Keep clear of the door zone of parked cars.
Never go up the inside of large vehicles at junctions.

p: Make sure your brakes, tyres and lights work, wear something easy to see, and consider a mirror or a bell. Never use your phone while riding.

title: Worried about seasickness on a ferry or your first cruise? What helps adults
description: Where to sit or book, what to eat, and what to do in the first queasy minutes at sea. Not medical advice.
intro: If you get seasick, a ferry crossing or a first cruise can feel like something to dread. A few choices before and during the trip make a real difference for many people. This is general information, not medical advice; a pharmacist can advise on travel sickness medicines.

list: Ask a pharmacist about travel sickness medicines well before you travel, as many need to be taken in advance and some cause drowsiness.
Check the forecast and, if you can, choose a calmer crossing time.
Get a good night of sleep and eat a light meal before you board.
The middle of the ship and the lower decks usually move least.
On a cruise, a cabin midship on a lower deck can help.
Get out on deck for fresh air if it is safe to do so.
Look at the horizon or a fixed point in the distance.
Avoid reading or looking at your phone for long periods.
Sip water, eat small plain snacks, and go easy on alcohol and heavy or greasy food.
Stop what you are doing and fix your eyes on the horizon.
Get to fresh air, or lie down and close your eyes.
Loosen tight clothing and take slow breaths.

p: After each trip, note where you sat, what you ate and what you did. Over a few journeys you will see what keeps you well, and you can plan the next trip around it.
See a GP if sickness is severe, lasts long after the journey, or comes with symptoms like a bad headache, chest pain or dizziness on dry land.

title: Why are my croissants dense, bready or leaking butter? A home baker's fault checklist
description: The common reasons homemade croissants fail, and how to change one thing at a time to get layers.
intro: Croissants are one of the hardest things to bake at home, and most people get a few dense or greasy batches before they get layers. The fault usually comes down to temperature, proofing or the oven. Change one thing at a time so you can tell what worked.

list: The butter may have melted into the dough during lamination. Keep dough and butter cold and similar in firmness, and chill between folds.
The butter may have been too hard and cracked into pieces; let it soften slightly so it bends without breaking.
Under-proofing is very common: croissants should look clearly puffy and wobble slightly before baking.
Usually over-proofing or proofing somewhere too warm, so the butter melts before the oven sets the layers. Proof somewhere cool enough that the butter stays solid.
An oven that isn't hot enough can let butter run out before the pastry sets; check it with an oven thermometer.
Bake on a preheated tray, and give them long enough to brown deeply.
Shape them evenly so the middles aren't much thicker than the ends.

p: Write down your flour, butter, dough and room temperatures, the number of folds and rests, the proof time and the oven temperature. Photograph the cut cross-section of each batch. Comparing batches side by side is the quickest way to see what made the difference.
Use oven gloves, and take care with hot trays and melted butter, which can burn.

title: Puppy crying in the crate at night? What to do in the first weeks
description: How to help a new puppy settle in the crate at night, tell a toilet whine from a protest, and make progress without giving up.
intro: Most puppies cry in the crate for the first few nights. It usually eases as they learn the crate is safe and that you're nearby. This is general information; if your puppy seems unwell or very distressed, speak to your vet.

list: Choose a crate big enough to stand, turn and lie stretched out, but not so big that one end becomes a toilet.
Put soft bedding in and cover part of it to make a den.
Many people start with the crate next to their bed, then move it gradually.

sections.h: Make the crate a good place by day
list: Feed meals and give chews in the crate with the door open.
Close the door for a few seconds while you sit nearby, then build up slowly.
Never use the crate as a punishment.
Young puppies often can't last the whole night. Take them out calmly, with little talk or play, then straight back.
If they've just been out, are comfortable and warm, and the crying starts as soon as you leave, it's more likely protest. A calm word or a hand near the crate can help them settle.
A puppy that has soiled the crate, is shaking, or seems unwell needs you, and possibly a vet.

p: Note how many minutes of crying each night and nap. Most owners see the numbers fall over a week or two, which makes the hard nights easier to get through.

If your puppy or dog panics, drools, or tries to escape the crate, or crying gets worse rather than better, speak to your vet or a qualified behaviourist. A dog that panics when left alone needs a different plan.

title: Heel pain on your first steps in the morning? What to track, and when to see a GP
description: A simple way to keep track of heel pain and what you've tried, so you and your GP or physio can see what's helping. Not medical advice.
intro: Heel pain that's worst on the first steps in the morning is common, especially in people who run, stand a lot or have changed their footwear. It often takes time to settle, and it's hard to tell what's helping. A short daily record makes that much clearer. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: The pain started after a fall or injury, or you can't put weight on your foot: get urgent advice.
You have swelling, numbness, tingling or a high temperature.
It hasn't improved after a few weeks of looking after it at home: see a GP or physio.
A 0-10 score for your first steps in the morning.
A 0-10 score in the evening, and roughly how long you were on your feet.
Any runs, long walks, hard floors or barefoot time.
List what you use: shoes, insoles, a night splint, stretches, ice.
Tick each one off on the days you do it, and note what it cost.
Try to change one thing at a time, and give each change a couple of weeks before judging it.

p: A few weeks of scores, what you did and what you tried gives your GP, physio or podiatrist a much clearer picture than memory alone.

title: How to get out of a timeshare safely (and avoid exit-company scams)
description: The routes owners use to leave a timeshare or points club, the risks of each, and the red flags to watch for. Not legal advice.
intro: Rising maintenance fees and changing plans leave many owners wanting out of a timeshare, and plenty of companies promise to get you out for a fee. Some routes are free; some carry real risks. This is general information, not legal or financial advice.

list: Read your contract for any surrender, hand-back or termination terms.
Ask the resort or owners' association in writing whether it has a hand-back or deed-back programme, and what it requires.
Ask whether hardship, age or health changes are taken into account.

p: Many timeshare contracts include a short cooling-off period during which you can cancel. Check your paperwork straight away and act within the deadline in writing.

list: Cold calls or messages claiming they can get you out or get your money back.
Large upfront fees before anything is done.
Pressure to stop paying your fees, or promises that sound guaranteed.
In the UK you can report suspected scams to Action Fraud; in the US, to the FTC.

sections.h: Think carefully before you stop paying
p: Stopping maintenance payments doesn't end the contract. It can lead to debt collection, legal action, foreclosure and damage to your credit. Get advice first.

list: Keep a dated record of every call, letter and reply.
UK: Citizens Advice can help with consumer contracts. US: your state consumer protection office or attorney general.
For complex contracts, speak to a qualified lawyer.

title: Gout keeps coming back? What to track between attacks
description: A simple gout diary: what to note during a flare and on the days in between, so you and your GP can spot patterns. Not medical advice.
intro: If you get repeat gout attacks, it can be hard to remember what came before each one. A short diary helps you and your GP see patterns and decide on treatment. This is general information, not medical or diet advice.

list: A joint is hot, swollen and very painful and you have a high temperature or feel unwell.
You've never had gout before and a joint suddenly becomes very painful and swollen.
Contact your GP if attacks are happening more often, or before changing any medicine.
Note which joint, the date it started, and pain on a 0-10 scale each day until it settles.
Note what you used to manage it and when, in your own words.
Alcohol, large or rich meals, and how much water you drank.
Hours on your feet, long journeys, sleep and illness.
Anything new: a new medicine, diet change or injury.

p: When a flare starts, look back at the three days before it. Over several attacks, patterns often become clearer than they feel from memory.
Bring your diary and any blood test results to your appointment. Ask your GP whether longer-term treatment is right for you.

title: How to stop creeping over the speed limit without noticing
description: Practical habits to stay under the limit, especially in 20mph zones, and how to keep track of licence points (UK).
intro: Most speeding tickets aren't for racing; they're for drifting a few mph over without noticing, often in 20mph or 30mph zones. A few habits make it much easier to stay under. This is general information, not legal advice.

list: Use a lower gear in 20mph zones, which makes it harder to drift up.
If your car has a speed limiter or cruise control, use it where it's safe and legal, and still watch the road and signs.
Leave a few minutes earlier so you're not tempted to make up time.
Most people creep on the same few roads: long straight 30s, downhill stretches, and roads where the limit drops.
Note those spots on your regular routes and check your speed as you approach them.

p: Sat-navs and apps sometimes show the wrong limit. Always follow the road signs, and look for repeater signs after junctions.

list: Speeding points usually stay on your licence for 4 years from the offence date.
If you reach 12 or more points within 3 years, you can be banned from driving.
If you passed your test in the last 2 years, 6 points can mean your licence is revoked.
Check your record on GOV.UK's 'View or share your driving licence information' service.

p: Never touch your phone while driving. Set any app or sat-nav up before you set off, and use a proper mount.

title: Failed the NCLEX? How to make a retake study plan from your performance report
description: A calm, practical way to plan an NCLEX-RN or NCLEX-PN retake: use your candidate performance report, focus on weak areas, and track progress.
intro: Failing the NCLEX is crushing, and many nurses who pass did not pass first time. A retake goes better with a plan built from what the exam told you, rather than doing more of the same. This is general information; always check your board of nursing's retake rules.

list: If you didn't pass, you'll receive a Candidate Performance Report showing how you did in each content area.
List each area as below, near or above the passing standard.
Your weakest areas get the most study time; don't neglect the others completely.
There is a waiting period before you can retake; check the current rules with your board of nursing and NCSBN.
Re-register and pay the fee, then pick a date that gives you enough time to prepare.
Count the days to your retake and share them out across content areas, weighted to your weak ones.
Mix content review with question practice every day.
Read the rationale for every question, right or wrong.
Log your scores for each practice block by content area.
Watch for areas that stay flat, and change how you study them.
Take full-length practice exams in exam conditions in the final weeks.

p: Plan rest days, keep your sleep regular in the run-up, and talk to someone you trust. If the stress feels overwhelming, speak to your GP or doctor.

title: Satin stitch not smooth? How to fix ragged edges, gaps and drifting stitches
description: Common satin stitch problems in hand embroidery and simple fixes to practise one at a time.
intro: Satin stitch looks simple but is one of the hardest stitches to get smooth. Most problems come down to a few things: stitch angle, spacing, edges and thread. Practising one small shape at a time and changing one thing at a time helps most stitchers improve quickly.

list: Outline the shape first in split stitch or back stitch, then satin stitch over the outline to get a raised, crisp edge.
Bring the needle up and down exactly on the line each time.
Draw a few guide lines across the shape at the angle you want.
Start in the middle of the shape and work out to one side, then go back and work the other side.
For wide shapes, change the angle gradually rather than all at once.
Place each stitch right next to the last, without overlapping.
Use fewer strands (often 1-3 for small shapes) for a smoother finish.
Keep an even tension and let your thread untwist now and then.

p: Long satin stitches snag and sag. Split big shapes into smaller sections, or use long-and-short stitch instead.
Stitch the same small leaf or petal shape a few times, photograph each one, and change one thing at a time. Comparing photos side by side makes it easy to see what's working.

title: Computer files a mess? How to organise your files and folders at home
description: A simple folder plan for personal files, a little-and-often way to sort the backlog, and habits that keep it tidy.
intro: Most home computers end up with a Desktop, Downloads folder and Documents folder full of files saved in random places. You don't need a perfect system; a simple folder plan and ten minutes a day is usually enough to get back in control.

p: Before a big clean-up, make a backup to an external drive or cloud service, so nothing important is lost by mistake.

list: Use no more than about ten top-level folders, named after areas of your life: Home, Money, Health, Work, Photos, Travel and so on.
Use one or two levels of sub-folders at most.
Put the year at the start of file names that matter, e.g. 2026-04 Car insurance.
Start with Downloads and Desktop, which are usually the worst.
Move ten files a day into the right folder, and delete what you don't need.
Check for duplicates before deleting anything you're unsure about.
Change your browser's download location or empty Downloads once a week.
Save new files straight into the right folder.
Use your computer's search for finding things, and good file names to make search work.

title: Psoriasis keeps flaring? How to track flares and treatments for your next appointment
description: A simple psoriasis diary: what to note each week, how to keep a treatment timeline, and when to see a doctor. Not medical advice.
intro: When psoriasis flares again and creams seem to stop working, it's hard to remember what you used, for how long, and what came before the flare. A short weekly record helps you and your GP or dermatologist decide what to try next. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Your psoriasis is spreading, very painful, or not responding to treatment.
Your joints are painful, stiff or swollen.
Get urgent help if your skin becomes red and inflamed over most of your body, or you feel unwell with a fever.
Score your patches, itch and soreness from 0 to 10.
Take a photo of the same spot in the same light.
Note anything unusual: stress, illness, cold weather, poor sleep, alcohol, a new soap or product.
For each cream, ointment, shampoo or light session, note when you started, how often you used it and when you stopped.
Note how your skin changed in the weeks after.
Bring the timeline to appointments so nothing gets missed.

p: When a flare starts, look back at the few weeks before. Patterns are often easier to see on paper than in memory.

sections.h: Don't change medicines on your own
p: Talk to your GP, pharmacist or dermatologist before stopping or changing any prescribed treatment.

title: Service charge gone up with no breakdown? How leaseholders can question it (England and Wales)
description: The steps leaseholders can take to understand and question a rising service charge, calmly and with evidence. Not legal advice.
intro: Service charges can rise sharply, and it isn't always clear what you're paying for. Leaseholders in England and Wales have rights to information and to challenge charges that aren't reasonable. This is general information, not legal advice.

list: Your lease sets out what can be charged for and how costs are shared.
Check what it says about the reserve fund, management fees and admin charges.
You can ask your landlord or managing agent in writing for a summary of the costs that make up the service charge.
You can then ask to inspect the invoices and receipts behind it.
Keep a copy of every request and note the date you sent it.
Put each year's budget and accounts side by side.
Note lines that jumped, lines with no visible work, and new lines with no explanation.
Talk to neighbours: a residents' association has more weight than one leaseholder.
Use the managing agent's complaints process, and its redress scheme if it belongs to one.
Service charges must be reasonable. In England you can apply to the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber); in Wales, the Leasehold Valuation Tribunal.
Before applying, get free initial advice from LEASE (the Leasehold Advisory Service) or Citizens Advice.

title: Setting up your child's first phone: a step-by-step guide for parents
description: How to set up the built-in controls, agree family rules together, and unlock apps in stages.
intro: A first phone is a big step, and most parents aren't sure what to allow or how to set it up. You don't need an expensive monitoring app to start: both iPhone and Android include parental controls, and a simple family agreement goes a long way.

list: iPhone: set up Family Sharing and Screen Time for your child's Apple account, with app limits, downtime and content restrictions.
Android: use Google Family Link to approve apps, set screen-time limits and set a bedtime.
Set a passcode only you know for these settings.
Agree where the phone lives at night (often outside the bedroom).
Agree when it's put away: meals, homework, bedtime.
Agree what to do if something upsetting happens online: tell a parent, no trouble.
Start with calls, texts to family and a few chosen apps.
Add the camera, group chats, video and other apps as trust builds.
Review together every week or two.
Lost or stolen phone: know how to locate, lock and wipe it.
Data or spending: turn off in-app purchases or require approval.
Upsetting messages or contact: keep the evidence, block and report, and in the UK report child sexual abuse concerns to CEOP. In an emergency call 999.

title: New hearing aids sound too loud or tinny? What to note for your follow-up appointment
description: Why new hearing aids often sound strange at first, what to write down, and how to get the most from your follow-up. Not medical advice.
intro: Many people find new hearing aids sound loud, sharp or tinny at first, because their brain hasn't heard those sounds for a long time. Some of it settles with regular wear, and some needs adjusting by your audiologist. Clear notes make that follow-up much more useful. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: You have sudden hearing loss, ear pain, discharge or bleeding.
You feel dizzy or have new ringing in one ear.
The aids rub, hurt or cause soreness that doesn't settle.
Follow the wear plan your audiologist gave you, often building up hours each day.
Start in quiet places at home, then move to busier ones.
Note how many hours you wore them each day.
Where you were and what you were doing.
What was wrong: too loud, tinny or metallic, your own voice sounds odd, whistling, hard to follow speech, uncomfortable.
How bad it was, from 0 to 10.

p: Sort your notes by how often each problem came up and take the top few to your appointment. Specific examples, like 'running water and cutlery sound harsh', are easier for an audiologist to adjust for than 'it sounds wrong'.
Many providers offer a trial or return period. Check the date on your paperwork and book follow-ups well before it ends.

title: Mind goes blank in exams even though you know the material? What to do
description: Practical ways to rehearse exam conditions, reset when you freeze, and keep one hard question from derailing the whole paper.
intro: Lots of people know their material at their desk and then freeze when the exam starts. Rehearsing the real conditions and having a simple plan for the moment you go blank makes a big difference for many students. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Do full practice papers at the same time of day as the exam, with a timer and no notes.
Sit somewhere unfamiliar if you can, like a library, to get used to a different room.
Practise the start: reading the instructions, choosing where to begin.
Put your pen down and sit back.
Breathe out slowly, a few times.
Say one short cue line to yourself, then start with the easiest part of the question.
Practise this in mocks so it's automatic on the day.

sections.h: Don't let one question take over
list: If you're stuck, mark it, move on and come back later.
Jot down anything you remember about the topic; it often unlocks the rest.
Keep your sleep, meals and exercise steady.
Plan the morning: what you'll eat, what you'll take, when you'll leave.

p: If panic attacks or anxiety are affecting your life, talk to your GP, doctor or a counsellor. Ask your college or exam body whether access arrangements are available.

title: Can't pop up when surfing? Floor drills to practise at home
description: Why the pop-up is so hard for new surfers, simple drills to practise on dry land, and what to check in a phone video.
intro: Getting from lying down to standing in one smooth move is the hardest part of learning to surf for most adults. Practising on dry land, where you can repeat it dozens of times, speeds things up a lot. This is general information; take lessons from a qualified instructor and surf safely.

list: Lie on the floor in your paddling position, chest up.
Place your hands flat under your chest, not on the edges of an imaginary board.
Push up and bring your back foot through first, then your front foot between your hands.
Land low, knees bent, looking forward, not down.
Ten minutes a day beats an hour once a week.
Do each step slowly until it's easy, then join them together.
Then practise the whole pop-up at speed.
Film from the side on your phone.
Look for: hands under your chest, back foot landing first, feet across the board, eyes forward.
Fix one thing at a time.
Pop up a fraction earlier, as the board starts to move with the wave.
Keep your weight centred so you don't nose-dive or stall.
Note after each session how many times you got to your feet and what went wrong.

p: Surf at lifeguarded beaches between the flags where you can, check conditions and tides, and stay in waves that suit your ability. If you have back, shoulder or heart problems, check with a doctor first.

title: Home gel nails chipping or peeling in days? The usual causes and how to fix them
description: The common reasons home gel manicures don't last, how to fix each one, and how to remove gel safely.
intro: Salon gel can last two weeks, but home sets often chip or peel within days. The cause is usually one of a few steps. Change one thing at a time and keep a note of how long each set lasts so you can see what helped.

list: Push back cuticles and remove any skin on the nail plate.
Lightly buff the shine off; don't over-buff, which thins nails.
Clean each nail with a dehydrator or alcohol wipe and keep fingers off them afterwards.
Apply thin coats; thick coats cure badly and peel.
Keep gel off your skin and cuticles; clean any off before curing.
Cap the free edge of the nail with each coat.
Check your lamp suits your gel; some gels need a particular type of lamp.
Cure each coat for the full time in the instructions.
Use a base, colour and top coat from the same system where you can.
Break the top coat, then soak in acetone (cotton pads and foil or clips) for long enough.
Gently push off softened gel; never peel or scrape it off.
Moisturise your nails and cuticles afterwards.

p: Uncured gel on skin can cause an allergy. If the skin around your nails becomes itchy, red or swollen, stop using gel and see a pharmacist or GP.

title: Tiling for the first time? Where to start, what to buy and how to avoid a wonky wall
description: A plain-English plan for a first small tiling job: set-out, kit, steps and when to call a professional.
intro: A splashback or small bathroom wall is a good first tiling job. Most problems come from rushing the set-out or skipping prep, not from the tiling itself. This is general information; leave electrics, gas and plumbing to qualified trades.

list: Measure the wall or floor and work out where the tiles will fall before you start.
Centre the layout so you don't end with thin slivers at the edges or around windows.
Fix a straight batten or draw a level line for your first row; walls and floors are rarely straight.
Check the adhesive suits your tiles and surface, and whether it's a wet area.
Use the trowel notch size the adhesive or tile instructions recommend.
You'll also need spacers, a level, a tile cutter, grout, a grout float and sealant.
Prepare the surface: clean, dry, sound and flat.
Spread adhesive over a small area at a time and press tiles on with spacers.
Check level and spacing every few tiles before the adhesive sets.
Leave the adhesive to set as instructed, then grout, clean off and seal with silicone at edges.
Cut wet or with a manual cutter where possible, and wear a dust mask and eye protection.
Leave moving sockets or switches, and any plumbing changes, to qualified trades.
For showers, get waterproofing checked by a professional.

p: Large floors, natural stone, very large tiles, or a whole wet room are tricky first jobs. If in doubt, get a quote and compare.

title: Can't stop picking your skin? Practical ways to cut down the urge
description: Why skin picking is so hard to stop, simple changes that make it harder to pick, and when to get help. Not medical advice.
intro: Picking at spots, bumps or skin around the nails is very common, and it can feel impossible to stop even when you want to. Small changes to your surroundings and noticing when the urge strikes help many people cut down. This is general information, not medical advice.

sections.h: Notice when and where it happens
list: Many people pick in the same places (the bathroom mirror, in bed, at a desk) and at the same times (tired, stressed, bored).
Jot down where you were and what you were doing each time you notice the urge.
After a week or two, the riskiest moments usually stand out.
Dim the bathroom light or cover a magnifying mirror.
Put tweezers and other tools out of easy reach.
Keep nails short and smooth, and wear plasters or gloves at risky times.

sections.h: Give your hands something else to do
list: Keep a fidget toy, stress ball or textured object where you usually pick.
When the urge comes, set a short timer and wait it out; urges often pass in a few minutes.

p: Slip-ups are normal. Count the days or areas you managed to leave alone rather than focusing on the times you picked.

See your GP if picked skin becomes red, hot, swollen or painful, or if picking is causing you distress or affecting daily life. Talking therapies such as habit reversal training can help, and your GP can advise on what's available.

title: Why doesn't my homemade curry taste like the takeaway?
description: The main differences between curry-house and home cooking, and what to change first, one thing at a time.
intro: Most British Indian restaurant curries are made differently from home recipes: a big batch of base gravy, very high heat, and each dish finished in minutes. Getting close at home usually means changing a few key things, one at a time.

list: Restaurants cook a large pot of onion-based gravy and use it as the start of most dishes.
Make a batch and freeze it in portions so each curry takes minutes.
Curry houses cook at very high heat with more oil than most home recipes.
Let the oil and spices sizzle briefly before adding gravy; don't let spices burn.
Reduce the sauce properly before adding more gravy.
Add whole spices and garlic-ginger paste first, ground spices next, and the base gravy after.
Many home curries taste raw because the spices didn't cook long enough in oil.

sections.h: Change one thing at a time
p: Keep a quick note after each cook: heat, oil, spice order, how long you reduced it, and how close it tasted to your takeaway. Change one thing next time.
Never leave hot oil unattended, keep a lid nearby, and never put water on an oil fire. Take care tilting pans near a gas flame.

title: A friend owes you money and won't pay it back? Steps to take (UK)
description: How to gather evidence, ask in writing, send a letter before claim, and use small claims if a friend won't repay. Not legal advice.
intro: Lending money to a friend can go wrong, and chasing it can feel awkward. A calm, written approach with good evidence gives you the best chance and keeps your options open. This is general information for England and Wales, not legal advice; rules differ elsewhere.

list: Bank transfers or receipts showing the money you gave.
Messages where they agreed it was a loan, promised to repay, or admitted they owe you.
A timeline of every promised repayment date and what happened.
Send a polite message asking for repayment by a specific date.
If nothing happens, send a firmer request with a final deadline.
Keep copies of everything you send and receive.

p: Before going to court, send a formal letter before claim setting out how much is owed, why, and the deadline to pay, and saying you'll start court action if they don't. Give them a reasonable time to respond.

sections.h: Is it worth going to court?
list: Can you show it was a loan, not a gift?
Do you know their current address?
Can they actually pay? A court judgment doesn't guarantee you'll be paid.
Court fees depend on the amount claimed; check the current fees on GOV.UK.

p: In England and Wales, many smaller money claims can be made online through the official Money Claim Online service. Citizens Advice can give free advice on your situation before you start.

title: How to deal with homesickness after moving to a new city or country
description: Practical ways to cope with homesickness when you've moved away, for university, work or a new country.
intro: Homesickness is very common after a move, even when the move was your choice. It usually comes in waves and eases as your new place starts to feel familiar. These are general ideas; if low mood lasts for weeks, talk to a doctor or student services.

list: Jot down when homesickness hits and what set it off: a call home, a holiday, a smell, a quiet evening.
Patterns help you plan for the hard moments rather than being caught out.

sections.h: Stay in touch, on a rhythm
list: Set regular call times that work across time zones, rather than calling every time you feel low.
Some people find a little less contact helps them settle; find what works for you.
Keep a few comfort items: photos, a favourite food, music, a familiar scent.
Find a shop or restaurant that sells food from home for the hardest days.

sections.h: Put down roots, one step at a time
list: Each week, try one small thing: a regular café, a class, a walk in a new area, saying yes to one invitation.
Join a group based on something you enjoy; expat and student groups can help too.

p: Birthdays, holidays and family events are often the hardest. Plan something for those days in advance, with people around you or a call home.
If you feel low most days for weeks, struggle to sleep or eat, or feel hopeless, talk to a doctor, your university's student services, or a support line.

title: First half marathon? A simple way to plan your training as a slow runner
description: How to build a first half marathon plan around three runs a week, your race date and your current fitness.
intro: Training plans for a half marathon vary hugely, which is confusing when it's your first. For most new runners the essentials are the same: build your long run gradually, keep most runs easy, and allow for missed weeks. If you have a health condition, check with your doctor before starting.

list: Note your race date and your current longest comfortable run.
Pick three days a week you can actually run.
If you can comfortably run 5-10K now, 12-16 weeks is a common amount of time to prepare.
One long run, building gradually week by week.
One easy run at a pace where you can talk.
One shorter run that's a little quicker, or run-walk intervals.
Increase the long run by small steps, and have an easier week every few weeks.
Run-walk is a perfectly good way to finish a half marathon.
If you miss a week, step back rather than jumping ahead.
Check the race cut-off time.
Practise with the shoes, kit and any drinks or snacks you'll use on the day.
Ease off in the final week or two so you start fresh.

p: Stop and get advice if you have chest pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness, or pain that doesn't settle.

title: How not to miss the northern lights: alerts, clouds and when to look
description: What aurora alerts mean, why clouds and the moon matter, and how to give yourself the best chance of seeing the northern lights.
intro: Most people miss the aurora because the alert arrives at the wrong moment, or because it's cloudy where they are. Knowing what to check, and having a plan, makes a big difference. No alert can guarantee a sighting.

list: Aurora alert services report geomagnetic activity; higher levels mean the aurora may be visible further from the poles.
Activity can rise and fall within minutes, so a live alert matters more than a daily forecast.
Clouds are the biggest reason people miss it: check a local cloud forecast as well as aurora activity.
A bright moon and city lights make it harder to see.
Find a dark spot with a clear view of the northern horizon (southern, if you're in the southern hemisphere).
Give your eyes 15-20 minutes to adjust, away from screens and lights.
A phone camera often picks up colour your eyes can't.
Turn on alerts and allow them to make a sound, if you want to be woken.
Have warm clothes and a plan ready so you can get outside quickly.

p: Dress for the cold, stay on public land, tell someone where you're going, and don't drive if you're very tired.

title: How to match clothes when you're colour blind
description: Simple ways to stop mixing up navy and black or blue and purple, and to shop for clothes with confidence.
intro: Many colour-blind people find clothes the most frustrating everyday problem: navy looks black, purple looks blue, and shop lighting makes it worse. A few habits make matching much easier.

list: Check the colour on each item's label or product page, or ask someone you trust.
Mark items with small tags or sort them into clearly separated sections by colour.
Keep confusable colours, like navy and black, on different rails or shelves.
Common mix-ups include navy and black, blue and purple, brown and green, and some reds and greens.
Make a short list of the pairs you personally get wrong and check those first.
Neutral basics (white, grey, black, denim) go with almost anything.
Patterns that include a colour you know make matching easier.
Keep a few tried-and-tested outfits that someone has checked.
Artificial shop lighting can change how colours look; check near a window if you can.
Read the colour name on the tag or ask a shop assistant.
Colour-identifier apps can help, but lighting affects them too.

title: Long flight with a toddler? An hour-by-hour plan to keep them busy
description: How to pace activities, snacks and screen time on a long flight with a 1 to 4 year old, and what to do if they melt down.
intro: The hardest part of flying with a toddler is usually not the first hour but the fifth. Pacing what you bring out, rather than using everything early, makes a long flight far more manageable. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Pack a few small, new or long-forgotten toys, wrapped if your child likes unwrapping.
Choose quiet activities with nothing that rolls under seats: sticker books, magnetic boards, crayons, small figures.
Check your airline's rules for strollers, car seats and baby food before you travel.
Let your toddler walk and run in quiet areas before boarding.
Think about whether to board early or late, depending on your child.
Plan one new thing roughly every 30-60 minutes: a toy, a snack, a book, an aisle walk, some screen time.
Save the most exciting items for the hardest stretch, often the middle or end of the flight.
Keep snacks small and frequent.
Change the scene: a short walk to the galley or back of the plane when the seatbelt sign is off.
Offer something new, a drink or a snack.
Most passengers understand; focus on your child, not the cabin.

sections.h: Don't medicate to make them sleep
p: Never give a child medicine to make them sleep unless a doctor has advised it. Ask a pharmacist or doctor about any health questions, including ear pain, before you fly.

title: How to stop catching an edge and start linking turns on a snowboard
description: Why new snowboarders catch an edge, what to practise, and how to link heel-side and toe-side turns.
intro: Catching an edge, where the downhill edge digs in and slams you down, is the classic beginner fall. It usually comes from a flat board, weight in the wrong place or looking down. A lesson from a qualified instructor is the quickest fix; these notes help you practise between lessons.

list: Riding with the board flat, so the downhill edge catches the snow.
Leaning back or looking at your feet.
Changing edge too slowly on gentle slopes.
Practise sliding on your heel edge, then your toe edge, across the slope.
Try the falling leaf: zigzag across the slope on one edge without turning down the hill.
Keep your knees bent and your weight over your front foot.
Look where you want to go; your shoulders and board follow.
Shift weight smoothly from one edge to the other, using your front foot to start the turn.
Start on very gentle terrain and build up.

p: Focus on one thing per run, and note after each lift how many turns you linked and which edge caught you. Take that list to your next lesson.
Wear a helmet, consider wrist guards and padded shorts, ride within your ability, and follow resort rules.

title: Price dropped right after you bought it? How to ask for the difference
description: What to check when something you've just bought gets cheaper, how to ask the store politely, and when returning and rebuying makes sense.
intro: It's frustrating to see something you just bought on sale days later. In most places you don't have a legal right to the difference, but many stores have their own price-drop or price-match policies, and a polite request often works. This is general information.

list: Look for a price-drop, price-protection or price-match policy on the store's website.
Note the window (often 7 to 30 days from purchase) and any exclusions such as clearance or marketplace sellers.
Keep your receipt or order confirmation.
Contact customer service with your order number, the date you bought it, and a link or screenshot showing the lower price.
Ask whether they can refund the difference as a goodwill gesture if there's no formal policy.
If you're still within the return period, returning and buying again at the lower price may be an option.
Count the cost first: return postage, restocking fees, and any discounts or gifts you'd lose.

p: Note each bigger purchase, the store's window and the date it ends, so you can check prices before it closes.

title: Out of packed lunch ideas? How to build a rotation your child will actually eat
description: A simple way to vary school lunches without waste: start from what they eat, rotate, and add one new thing at a time.
intro: Many parents end up packing the same few things every day because they know they'll get eaten. A short rotation built from foods your child already likes, plus the odd small new swap, adds variety without lunches coming home untouched.

list: For a week, note what comes home uneaten.
List the foods your child reliably eats: bread or wraps, fillings, fruit, vegetables, snacks.
Build lunches mainly from that list.
Plan two or three weeks of lunches and repeat them.
Swap the format, not just the food: a sandwich one day, a wrap or crackers and fillings the next.
Change one item at a time.
Put a small amount of something new next to familiar foods.
Don't worry if it comes back; try it again another week.
Many schools are nut-free or limit sweets and fizzy drinks; check your school's food policy.
Use an ice pack for foods that need to stay cool.

p: On Sunday, make a short shopping list and prepare anything that can be made ahead or frozen, so weekday mornings are quicker.

title: What makes dry eyes worse? How to find your own triggers
description: Common things that make dry eyes feel worse, and a simple way to work out which ones matter for you.
intro: Dry eyes often feel better some days and worse on others, and it can be hard to see why. Keeping short notes for a few weeks can show patterns you can talk through with your optician, pharmacist or eye doctor. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: Long spells looking at a screen, when people tend to blink less.
Dry air from heating or air conditioning, fans, and air vents in cars or on planes.
Wind, smoke and dust.
Contact lenses, especially when worn for long hours.
Short or poor sleep.
Some medicines. If you think a medicine is affecting your eyes, ask a pharmacist or doctor before changing it.
Score how your eyes feel morning and evening, for example from 0 (fine) to 10 (very bad).
Note screen hours, where you spent the day (heating, air conditioning, outdoors), sleep, and contact lens hours.
Write down every drop, gel, compress or treatment you used and when.

sections.h: Change one thing at a time
list: If you want to test something, change only one thing for about two weeks so you can see whether it makes a difference.
Changing several things at once makes it hard to tell which one helped.

p: Get urgent medical help if you have sudden eye pain, a sudden change in your vision, or a red eye that is getting worse.

title: Dry eye drops not working? What to note before your next appointment
description: If you've tried several drops and nothing seems to help, here's what to write down so your next eye appointment is more useful.
intro: Many people with dry eyes try drop after drop and can't tell what is helping. Your optician or eye doctor can do more with a clear record than with a memory of 'I've tried everything'. This is general information, not medical advice.

list: The name of each drop, gel or ointment, how often you used it and for how long.
Warm compresses, eye masks, lid cleaning, or clinic treatments, with dates.
Anything that made your eyes sting or feel worse.
A daily score morning and evening for two to four weeks.
When it's worst: on waking, at the screen, in the car, outdoors.
Other symptoms such as blurred vision that clears when you blink, light sensitivity or sticky eyes in the morning.
What you spend each month on drops and treatments.
This helps when you ask about options or cheaper alternatives.
What type of dry eye do I have?
How long should I try this before deciding whether it works?
Is there anything in my daily routine I should change?

p: Get urgent medical help if you have sudden eye pain, a sudden change in your vision, or a red eye that is getting worse.

title: What to do with all your kids' school artwork (without the guilt)
description: A simple routine for the piles of art that come home: display, photograph, keep a few, and let the rest go.
intro: Children can bring home a lot of artwork, and it's normal to feel guilty about throwing any of it away. A simple routine keeps the pieces that matter and stops the rest taking over the house.

list: Pick one tray, basket or folder where new artwork goes when it comes home.
Clear it once a week or once a fortnight, not every day.
Put a few pieces on the fridge, a wall strip or a frame you can swap.
When something new goes up, the old piece moves on to the next step.
Take a photo of each piece with your child's name and the date.
Keep a small number of originals each term: the ones your child is proudest of, or that mark a milestone.
Recycle the rest once they're photographed. Ask your child to choose their favourites; many children are happy once they've chosen.
Store kept originals flat in one labelled box or folder per child per year.
Back up the photos somewhere other than your phone.

p: If you share artwork with family, use a private album rather than public social media, especially if it shows your child's name or school.

title: How to stop getting street-cleaning tickets
description: Practical ways to remember street-sweeping and alternate-side parking days when you park on the street.
intro: Street-cleaning tickets often happen to people who know the rule but forget on the day. A couple of habits and reminders cut the risk a lot. This is general information, not legal advice; always follow the posted signs.

sections.h: Read the sign where you parked
list: Check the day, the time window and whether the rule applies to your side of the street.
Some streets have different rules on each side, or on alternating weeks.
Take a photo of the sign so you can check it later.
One the evening before, when you can still find another spot easily.
One about an hour before the cleaning window starts.
Many cities publish street-cleaning schedules and offer email or text alerts.
Rules can be suspended on public holidays or in bad weather; check your city's announcements.

sections.h: Park with the schedule in mind
list: If you can, choose a spot whose cleaning day is furthest away.
When you move the car, note the new sign and update your reminder.

title: Stuck on 6.5 in IELTS Writing? What to change before you retake
description: If your Writing score keeps landing half a band short, here's how to work out why before you pay for another test.
intro: Many test takers get the same Writing band attempt after attempt. Retaking without changing how you prepare often gives the same result. This guide is general advice and is not connected to the organisations that run the test.

sections.h: Look at what's been the same each time
list: Write down every result by section, with dates.
Collect the essays you wrote in practice before each test.
Note what you did differently, if anything, between attempts.

sections.h: Check your essays against the four public criteria
list: The published Writing band descriptors cover task achievement or task response, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, and grammatical range and accuracy.
Rate several of your practice essays against each one, ideally with a teacher, to see which is lowest most often.
Task 2 counts for more of the Writing score than Task 1, so weaknesses there matter more.

sections.h: Fix one thing at a time
list: Keep a list of mistakes you repeat, such as missing a part of the question, unclear paragraphs, or the same grammar errors.
Spend most of your practice on the weakest criterion for a few weeks.
Write under timed conditions so practice matches the real test.
Check your recent practice essays are consistently meeting the level you need, not just once.
If you think a past result was marked wrongly, ask your test centre about a re-mark (Enquiry on Results) and its fee.
Some centres offer a one-skill retake for certain test types; check with your centre and with the organisation you're applying to whether it's accepted.

title: Which IELTS Writing criterion is holding your band down?
description: A simple way to rate your own essays against the four public Writing criteria and find the one to work on.
intro: Your Writing band comes from four criteria, and being half a band short often means one of them is lower than the rest. Rating your own essays against each one can show where to focus. This is general advice and not connected to the organisations that run the test.

list: Task achievement (Task 1) or task response (Task 2): did you answer every part of the question fully?
Coherence and cohesion: is it organised clearly, with logical paragraphs and linking?
Lexical resource: is your vocabulary varied, accurate and suitable?
Grammatical range and accuracy: do you use a mix of sentence structures with few errors?
Read the public band descriptors for the band you need and the one below.
For each essay, give each criterion a score and write one sentence on why.
Do this for at least five essays; one essay isn't enough to see a pattern.
The criterion that is lowest most often is usually the one to work on first.
If your scores vary a lot, timing or planning may be the problem rather than language.

p: Self-rating has limits. If you can, ask a teacher to rate the same essays and compare their scores with yours.

title: How to cut hair at home without it looking DIY
description: Practical tips for cutting your own or your family's hair with clippers or scissors, and avoiding the most common mistakes.
intro: Cutting hair at home can save money, but uneven results put many people off. Going slowly, starting longer and working in sections makes a big difference.

list: Clippers with a set of guards for short cuts.
Proper hairdressing scissors for trims; kitchen scissors tend to give ragged ends.
A comb, clips to section hair, and two mirrors or a phone camera to see the back.
With clippers, start with a higher guard number than you want; you can go shorter, but not longer.
With scissors, cut small amounts and check before cutting more.
Divide the hair into sections and finish one before moving on.
Compare both sides often, in the mirror and by feeling lengths between your fingers.
Cutting wet hair too short: hair can look longer when wet, especially if it's curly.
Pressing the clippers into the head, which can take off more than expected.
Rushing the back and around the ears.

p: Write down the guard numbers or lengths you used, so the next cut is quicker and more consistent.

title: Bedroom too hot to sleep? How to cool it down without air con
description: Simple ways to keep a bedroom cooler in hot weather: when to open windows, when to close curtains, and what helps at night.
intro: In hot weather many homes, especially new builds and top-floor flats, stay warm long into the night. The biggest wins usually come from keeping heat out during the day and letting cooler air in at the right time. This is general information.

sections.h: Keep the sun out during the day
list: Close curtains or blinds on windows that get direct sun, before the room heats up.
Light-coloured or blackout curtains help; outside shading helps most if you have it.

sections.h: Open windows only when it's cooler outside
list: Check the temperature outside and inside; a cheap thermometer for the room helps.
When it's hotter outside than in, keep windows closed.
Open them in the evening and overnight once it's cooler outside, and if it's safe to do so. Opening windows on opposite sides of the home can create a through-draught.
Use a fan to move air, ideally near an open window when it's cooler outside.
Switch to light bedding, such as a low-tog duvet or just a sheet.
Turn off lights and electronics you don't need, as they add heat.

p: Drink plenty of water in hot weather. If you or someone you live with feels unwell in the heat, for example dizzy, confused or very weak, get medical help; in an emergency call your local emergency number.

title: Why won't my calves grow? What to log before you change anything
description: If your calves stay the same size however much you train, here's what to track so you can see what's really happening.
intro: Calves are a common sticking point. Genetics play a big part, but many people also train them inconsistently or change their routine too often to tell what works. A few weeks of simple notes gives you a clearer picture. This is general training information, not medical advice.

list: The exercise: straight-leg raises (standing) work mainly the gastrocnemius; bent-knee raises (seated) work more of the soleus underneath.
Load, sets and reps.
Whether you used the full range of motion: a full stretch at the bottom and a full rise at the top.
How close to failure you went.
Calf girth at the same spot, measured the same way (see the measuring guide).
A photo from the same angle, distance and lighting.
Body weight, since calf size often changes with overall weight.

sections.h: Change one thing at a time
list: Keep the same routine for at least four weeks before judging it.
If nothing has changed, adjust one variable: frequency, load, rep range, range of motion or exercise choice.
Changing everything at once makes it impossible to know what helped.
Some people's calves grow slowly whatever they do; that's normal.
If you have sudden pain, swelling or redness in one calf, get medical advice promptly rather than training through it.

title: How to measure your calves accurately so the tape is honest
description: A simple, repeatable way to measure calf size so you can tell whether your training is working.
intro: Small differences in how you measure can hide or invent changes. Measuring the same way every time matters more than the exact method.

list: Measure at the same time of day, ideally in the morning before training.
Don't measure straight after a workout, when muscles can look and measure bigger for a while.
Use a flexible tape measure that doesn't stretch.
Stand with your weight spread evenly on both feet and your calves relaxed.
Measure around the widest part of the calf.
Note how far that spot is from the floor or the back of the knee, so you can find it next time.
Keep the tape level all the way round and snug, without squashing the skin.
Take three readings and use the middle one.
Measure both legs; it's normal for them to differ slightly.

p: Measure once a month and add a photo from the same angle. Real changes in muscle size are slow, so look at the trend over several months.

title: Your child understands your language but answers in English? What helps
description: Gentle, practical ways to get more replies in your family's language, without turning it into a fight.
intro: It's very common for children growing up with two languages to understand the home language but reply in the language of school and friends. It usually means they need more reasons and chances to use it, not that the language is lost.

list: Use the language as much as you can at home, in everyday routines, not just for instructions.
Add books, songs, audiobooks and shows in your language.
Time with relatives and other children who speak it counts a lot.

sections.h: Create a real need to use it
list: Video calls with grandparents or relatives who don't speak the majority language well.
A daily routine, game or time of day that happens only in your language.
Trips or playdates where your language is the one everyone uses.
Repeat back what they said in your language, then carry on the conversation.
Try 'How do you say that in ...?' as a game, not a test.
Praise attempts; avoid making it a punishment or battle.
Note roughly how many of their replies are in your language each week. Small increases over months are real progress.

p: Growing up with two languages doesn't cause speech problems. If you're concerned about how your child speaks or understands in any language, talk to a speech and language therapist or your child's doctor.

title: A warning light came on in your car: what to do
description: What dashboard warning light colours usually mean, which ones mean stop, and how to get it checked without panic.
intro: A warning light can be alarming if you don't know cars. Most cars use a colour system, and your car's handbook explains each symbol. This is general information; always follow your handbook and, if in doubt, stop safely and get help.

list: A red warning light usually means a serious problem. Stop as soon as it's safe to do so, switch off the engine if the handbook says to, and get help.
Examples include oil pressure, engine temperature, brake system, and battery or charging warnings.

sections.h: Amber usually means get it checked
list: An amber or yellow light usually means something needs checking soon.
A steady engine management (check engine) light means get it checked as soon as you can.
A flashing engine management light can mean a more serious fault. Reduce speed and get it checked straight away; stop if the car feels wrong.
These usually just show that something is on, such as headlights or cruise control.
Note the symbol, its colour, whether it's steady or flashing, and what the car was doing when it came on.
Take a photo of the dashboard if it's safe.
Many garages can read the fault code for you; ask what the code means and for a written quote before agreeing to repairs.

title: How to hit your protein target without going over your calories
description: Practical ways to close a daily protein gap when you're also watching calories.
intro: If you're aiming for a protein target and a calorie limit at the same time, the trick is choosing foods that give more protein for their calories, and planning so you're not left with a big gap at the end of the day. This is general information, not nutrition advice; if you have kidney disease, are pregnant or follow a medical diet, ask your doctor or a dietitian.

list: Include a protein source at every meal and snack, rather than trying to catch up at dinner.
Check your running total mid-afternoon, while there's still time to adjust.
Look at the label: divide grams of protein by calories, then multiply by 100 to get protein per 100 calories.
Lean meat and poultry, white fish, egg whites, low-fat Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, tofu and lentils often score well.
Fattier versions of the same foods usually give less protein per calorie.
Replace part of a meal with a higher-protein option instead of adding extra food on top.
For example, choose a higher-protein yogurt or bread, or add beans or lentils in place of some of the rice or pasta.

sections.h: Keep a few gap fillers ready
list: Have two or three foods you like that fit a small calorie budget, so the evening gap is easy to close.
Note which ones you actually eat, so your list stays realistic.

title: How to work out protein per 100 calories (and why it helps)
description: A simple calculation from the food label that shows which of your usual foods give the most protein for their calories.
intro: Comparing foods by protein per 100 grams can mislead you when you're watching calories. Protein per 100 calories shows how much protein you get for the calories you spend. This is general information, not nutrition advice.

list: Find the protein (grams) and energy (kcal) for the same amount on the label, for example per 100 g or per serving.
Divide protein by calories, then multiply by 100.
Example: a food with 10 g of protein and 100 kcal gives 10 g of protein per 100 calories.
Work it out for the foods you already buy and eat, not a generic list.
Sort them from highest to lowest; the top of the list are your best gap fillers.

p: Protein per calorie is one useful number, not the only one. Fibre, vegetables and foods you enjoy matter too, and a dietitian can help if you need a plan for a health condition.

title: How to stop scrolling for ages deciding what to watch
description: Simple ways for couples and families to choose something to watch in minutes instead of losing the evening.
intro: With several streaming services, choosing what to watch can take longer than the show. A bit of preparation and a simple rule for the evening makes it much quicker.

list: Whenever someone recommends a show or film, add it to one list straight away, whichever service it's on.
Note which service it's on and roughly how long it is.
Agree how much time you have tonight before you start looking.
Pick the mood: something light, gripping, or familiar.
Each person suggests up to three options from the list.
Each person can veto one.
Choose from what's left, or take turns choosing on different nights.

sections.h: Keep track of what you've watched
list: Mark shows as finished, abandoned or in progress, so you don't revisit the same options every night.
Set a time limit for choosing, such as five minutes; if nothing's chosen, go back to something you're halfway through.

title: How to keep track of newborn feeds (and which side you fed on)
description: Simple ways to remember when your baby last fed and which side, and to share it with whoever is helping.
intro: In the early weeks it's very hard to remember when the last feed was, especially at night. A simple record helps you and anyone helping you. This is general information; follow advice from your midwife, health visitor or doctor about how often and how much your baby should feed.

list: The time each feed started.
Which side you started on, or whether it was a bottle.
Anything you want to remember, such as a sleepy feed or a long gap.
Use whatever is quickest at 3am: a phone note, an app, or a sheet of paper by the bed.
Some parents move a hair tie or bracelet to the side they'll start on next time.
Keep the record somewhere everyone helping can see, so nobody has to ask.
Agree who logs feeds when someone else does a bottle.

p: Contact your midwife, health visitor or doctor if you're worried about your baby's feeding, weight, wet or dirty nappies, or if your baby seems unwell.

title: How to restart a stalled thesis after weeks or months away
description: Practical steps to get back into thesis or dissertation writing when you've lost momentum.
intro: Many graduate students hit long stretches where the thesis doesn't move. Getting going again is usually about making the next step very small and very clear, not about finding a burst of motivation. This is general advice; if low mood or anxiety is stopping you working, talk to your university's support services or a doctor.

list: Open every file and list what exists: chapters, drafts, notes, data.
For each chapter, write one line on what 'done' would mean.
Mark what's finished, what's drafted and what hasn't been started.
Pick one section and one small task, such as 'rewrite the first paragraph of 3.2' or 'list the five sources for this section'.
Work for a short, fixed time, such as 25 minutes, and stop.
At the end of each session, write down exactly what you'll do next time.
This makes it much easier to start again, even after a break.
Work back from your submission date using the pace you actually manage, not your ideal pace.
Tell your supervisor where you are and agree the next milestone; most supervisors would rather hear early.

p: Writing groups, writing retreats and your university's writing centre can all help. You don't have to restart alone.

title: How to write a weekly progress update for your thesis supervisor
description: A short, honest template for keeping your supervisor informed, especially when progress has been slow.
intro: A short regular update keeps your supervisor in the loop and makes meetings more useful. It also helps you see your own progress. Keep it brief; one page is plenty.

list: What you did this week: sections drafted or revised, reading, analysis.
Time spent and words written, if you track them.
What got in the way.
What you plan to do next week.
Any questions or decisions you need from your supervisor.
If little happened, say so briefly and say what the next small step is.
Supervisors can help much more when they know early that you're stuck.
Send it on the same day each week, even if it's short.
Keep a copy of every update; together they show your progress over months.

title: How to share baby photos privately with family far away
description: Ways to let grandparents and relatives see your baby's photos without posting them on social media.
intro: Many parents want family to see every new photo but would rather not post them on social media. There are simple ways to share privately; the key is controlling who has access and agreeing a few ground rules.

list: Use a shared album that only invited people can see, rather than a public or semi-public profile.
Check whether viewers need an account; for some grandparents a simple link is easiest.
Check what the service does with your photos and whether you can export or delete them.
Ask relatives not to repost photos on social media without asking.
Explain why, kindly; most family members are happy to respect it once they know.
Review who has access every so often and remove anyone who no longer needs it.
Remember that no service can stop screenshots, so only invite people you trust.

p: Back up the originals somewhere other than your phone, so they're safe whatever happens to the sharing service.

title: How to share school pickups and kids' activities with your partner (so it's not all in one head)
description: A simple weekly routine for couples to agree who is doing each pickup, drop-off and activity.
intro: In many households one parent ends up holding the whole family schedule in their head. A short weekly check-in and a clear 'who's doing it' for each job makes things fairer and means fewer missed pickups.

list: Go through the coming week together: school, clubs, appointments, work travel.
Give every pickup and drop-off a named person, not 'one of us'.
Use one place both of you actually look at, whether a shared calendar, an app or a whiteboard.
Write the person's name on each item.
If plans change, update the shared view straight away and tell the other person.
Agree how to ask for a swap, so it's easy rather than awkward.

sections.h: Share the planning, not just the driving
p: Take turns being the one who checks the week ahead, so the mental load doesn't always sit with the same person.

title: How to work out your real hourly pay delivering, after gas
description: A simple way for delivery and rideshare drivers to see what they actually clear per hour after gas, miles and waiting time.
intro: The pay shown in delivery apps doesn't include your gas, the wear on your car, or the time spent waiting and driving back. Working out your own figure takes a few minutes per shift. This is general information, not financial or tax advice.

list: The time you started and finished, including waiting and driving between orders.
Your odometer reading at the start and end.
What each app paid you, including tips.
Gas: miles driven divided by your car's miles per gallon, multiplied by the price per gallon.
Wear and other costs: choose a per-mile figure for maintenance, tyres and depreciation; use the same figure every time.
Add the two to get your cost for the shift.
Take total pay, subtract your costs, and divide by the total hours, from start to finish.
Compare shifts by time of day and by app to see which are worth it for you.

p: Never use your phone to log or check offers while driving. Record numbers when you're parked.

title: Cost per mile for delivery drivers, explained
description: What goes into the cost of each mile you drive for delivery apps, and how to estimate your own figure.
intro: Every mile you drive for a delivery or rideshare app costs you money, even when it doesn't feel like it. Knowing your own cost per mile helps you judge whether an offer is worth taking. This is general information, not financial or tax advice.

list: Gas, which changes with fuel prices and your car's efficiency.
Maintenance: oil changes, brakes, tyres.
Depreciation: your car loses value as the miles go up.
Insurance and other running costs, if you count part of them.

sections.h: Estimate your gas cost per mile
list: Divide the price of a gallon by your car's real miles per gallon.
Example: $3.50 a gallon at 25 mpg is 14 cents a mile in gas.
Look at what you spent on maintenance and tyres over the last year and divide by miles driven.
Add a figure for depreciation if you want a fuller picture.
Multiply the offer's total miles (including the drive back) by your cost per mile.
Subtract that from the pay to see what you'd really keep. Only check offers when parked.

title: How to convert oven times to air fryer times
description: A simple starting point for turning oven temperatures and times into air fryer settings, and how to check food is cooked.
intro: Most packets and recipes give oven instructions only. Air fryers usually cook faster because they circulate hot air closely around the food, so you generally need a lower temperature and a shorter time. Models vary, so treat any conversion as a starting point and always check food is cooked through.

list: Reduce the oven temperature by about 20°C (around 25°F).
Reduce the time by about 20%, then check early.
Many packets now include air fryer instructions too; use those when they're given.
Check part-way through and shake the basket or turn the food so it browns evenly.
Don't overfill the basket; food cooks more evenly in a single layer.
Meat, poultry and fish must be cooked through. A food thermometer is the most reliable check.
Reheated food should be piping hot all the way through.
Follow the food-safety advice on the packet.

p: Write down what worked for each food in your fryer: temperature, time, and whether you'd change it. After a few weeks you'll have settings you can trust.

title: How to send a fax without a fax machine
description: Options for sending the occasional fax for forms and paperwork when you don't own a fax machine or landline.
intro: Some banks, insurers, medical offices and government agencies still ask for signed forms by fax. You don't need a fax machine; there are several ways to send one occasionally.

list: Ask whether they accept the form by secure upload, email or post instead.
If fax is the only option, check the exact fax number and whether a cover page is needed.
Online fax services and apps: you upload a scan or photo and they send it. Some have free options with limits or adverts; others charge per fax or by subscription.
Print and shipping shops often send faxes for a per-page fee.
Some public libraries offer fax services.
Photograph the pages flat, in good light, with no shadows.
Make sure signatures and small print are readable.
Send pages in the right order.
Check the service's privacy terms before sending medical, financial or ID documents.
Keep the delivery confirmation as proof it was sent.

title: Car sick in the back seat? Why it happens and what adults can try
description: Why many adults still get car sick as back-seat passengers, and simple things to try on the next trip.
intro: Plenty of adults still get car sick, especially in the back seat. It usually happens when your eyes and your inner ear disagree about movement: your body feels the car moving, but your eyes are fixed on something still, like the seat in front or a phone. This is general information, not medical advice.

sections.h: Why the back seat is often worse
list: From the back you often can't see the road ahead, so your eyes get less warning of turns and braking.
Looking down at a phone, book or the seat in front adds to the mismatch.
Sit in the front passenger seat if you can, or a middle back seat where you can see out of the windscreen.
Look ahead at the horizon or the road rather than out of the side windows.
Avoid reading or screens; try audiobooks, podcasts or music instead.
Get fresh air: open a window a little or point an air vent at your face.
Eat something light before the trip and avoid heavy, greasy or spicy food.
A pharmacist can tell you about travel sickness remedies and when to take them before a journey.
Some remedies cause drowsiness, so check before using them if you need to drive later.

p: Note your seat, what you ate, whether you used a screen and how you felt on each trip. Patterns often show up within a few journeys.
See a doctor if you feel dizzy or sick when you're not travelling, or if symptoms are new, severe or getting worse.

title: Wifi not reaching upstairs? What to try first
description: Free fixes to try before buying an extender or mesh system, and how to choose if you need one.
intro: Wifi often struggles to reach rooms far from the router, especially through thick walls and floors. Before buying anything, a few free changes can make a real difference.

list: Run a speed test on your phone in each room and note the results.
Test at the same time of day so the results are comparable.
Move the router somewhere central and higher up, not on the floor or inside a cupboard.
Keep it away from thick walls, mirrors, fish tanks, microwaves and large metal objects.
Restart the router, and check for updates if your provider's app offers them.
Re-test each room after each change.
Wifi extenders repeat the signal; they're cheap but can reduce speed.
Powerline adapters send the connection through your electrical wiring; results depend on the wiring.
Mesh systems use several units to cover the whole home; usually the most reliable but cost more.

p: If your provider offers a booster for a monthly fee, compare the total cost over a year or two with buying a device outright, and check how long the contract lasts.

title: How to find a pen pal for real letters, safely
description: Ways for adults to find a pen pal for handwritten letters, and how to stay safe while doing it.
intro: Swapping real letters can be a lovely way to make a friend. You don't need to give out your home address to do it, and a few simple habits keep it safe and enjoyable.

list: Established pen pal clubs and letter-writing groups.
Postcard-swapping projects, if you'd like to start small.
Hobby groups and magazines that run pen pal sections.
Consider using a PO box or a mail forwarding service instead of your home address.
Don't share your address until you're comfortable, and only through a trusted service.
Never send money, gift cards or bank details to a pen pal, whatever the reason.
Be wary of anyone who quickly turns the friendship romantic or asks for help with money.
Keep personal details such as your workplace and daily routine to yourself.
Agree roughly how often you'll write, so nobody feels ignored.
Share small everyday things; that's what makes letters fun to receive.

title: How to go vegetarian gradually when everyone around you eats meat
description: A step-by-step way to cut down on meat and stick with it, even when family, friends and colleagues don't.
intro: Going vegetarian or vegan overnight works for some people, but many find a gradual approach easier to stick with, especially when the people around them eat meat. This is general information, not nutrition advice; talk to a doctor or dietitian if you're pregnant, have a health condition or are worried about nutrients.

list: Pick a first step you can manage, such as two meat-free days a week.
Move up only when that feels normal: more days, then cutting out one type of meat at a time.
Some people go from red meat, to poultry, to fish, to none.
List the meals you already eat often.
Find a meat-free version of each one, such as bean chilli, lentil bolognese or vegetable curry.
Changing familiar meals is easier than learning a whole new way of eating.
Work lunches: check the menu in advance or bring something.
Family meals: offer to cook a dish everyone can eat.
Barbecues and parties: bring something you'll enjoy and can share.
If you eat meat, note what was happening: hunger, tiredness, social pressure, or no other option.
Plan for that situation next time instead of giving up.

p: A varied diet matters. If you're cutting out animal products, read up on nutrients like B12, iron and protein, and ask a doctor or dietitian if you're unsure.

title: What to eat at work lunches and barbecues when you're going veggie
description: Practical ideas for social meals when you're going vegetarian or vegan and the others aren't.
intro: Social meals are where many people slip when they're cutting out meat. A little planning makes it much easier to enjoy the occasion without being stuck with a side salad.

list: Look at the menu online before you go and choose in advance.
Many cuisines have plenty of meat-free dishes, such as Indian, Middle Eastern, Mexican and Italian.
If the options are poor, eat something filling beforehand.
Bring something to grill that you'll enjoy, such as veggie burgers, halloumi (if you eat dairy), corn on the cob or vegetable skewers.
Ask for your food to be cooked on a separate part of the grill or on foil if that matters to you.
Bring enough to share; it's often popular.
Offer to bring a main dish so you know there's something to eat.
Let the host know in advance, kindly and simply.

p: You don't have to explain or debate your choice. A short, friendly answer is enough, then change the subject.

title: How to build a habit of praying the five daily prayers on time
description: Practical, gentle ways to become more consistent with daily prayers, especially after a break.
intro: Many Muslims find it hard to keep all five daily prayers on time, especially after a busy period or a break. Small, practical steps often help more than trying to change everything at once. This is practical guidance, not religious rulings; for questions about rulings, ask a scholar or imam you trust.

list: Notice which prayer you miss most often and why: sleep, work, travel or simply forgetting.
Focus on getting that one on time for a couple of weeks, then add the next.
Link each prayer to something you already do, such as a meal, a break or arriving home.
Set reminders a little before each prayer time, not just at the start.
Keep a prayer mat somewhere you'll see it, at home and at work if you can.
Plan where you'll pray when you're out, travelling or at work.
Pray with family, a friend or at the mosque when you can.
A friend to check in with can help keep you going.

p: If you miss a prayer, return to the next one rather than giving up. For questions about making up missed prayers, ask a scholar or imam you trust.

title: Why you rush the beat, and how to practise timing
description: Practical exercises for players who rush or drag, even after practising with a metronome.
intro: Rushing or dragging is one of the most common problems for self-taught players, and it's often hard to hear while you're playing. Practising with a metronome helps, but how you use it matters.

list: Record a short passage against a click and listen back.
It's much easier to hear rushing or dragging on a recording than while playing.
Practise at a tempo where you can play cleanly and stay locked to the click.
Speed up only a few beats per minute at a time.
Count or tap the eighth or sixteenth notes between the beats.
Set the click to subdivisions until you feel them without it.
